FinanceTab.title: Norse Atlantic suspends all flights as it faces potential collapse
FinanceTab.text:
The Norwegian low cost carrier Norse Atlantic Airways has suspended all flights as it rushes to resolve what it warned is a critical financial situation.

The airline said if no solution can be found, it intends to file for bankruptcy.

The airline uses a fleet of 12 Boeing 787 aircraft on long-haul routes from a number of European airports, including London Gatwick, Rome and Oslo.

Prior to the suspension of flights, it was advertising services from London to Orlando, Cape Town, Bangkok and Phuket.

One aircraft was meant to depart London for Orlando this morning, while another was meant to arrive from Cape Town this evening.

The suspension has also affected Pakistan International Airlines, which had been leasing aircraft and crews from Norse Atlantic.

PIA was forced to cancel services from London to Islamabad and from Manchester to Lahore last night.

In a statement on social media, PIA said all UK flights from today would be operated by aircraft from its own fleet.

Londoner Fred was due to fly to Cape Town with Norse Atlantic next week for a friend's wedding, but has decided to change his plans.

"Yesterday the exact same flight I was going to get was cancelled, so I was worried" he told the BBC's Your Voice. "I sent an email to Norse and have had nothing back".

He decided to rebook with a different airline, which cost him an extra £1,000.

Another traveller, Claire from Herefordshire, is currently on holiday in South Africa with her daughter.

"We are due to fly home on Sunday and are now looking at a really expensive flight back," she said.

"We have tried contacting Norse but have been given an automated response saying someone will get back to us within three business days."

Consumer group Which? advised Norse Atlantic customers to not cancel their flights as the airline has not collapsed. Doing so removes passengers' right to a refund.

Rory Boland, Which? travel editor, said: "If Norse does go bust, whether you get a refund depends on how you booked and paid. If you booked directly with Norse, you may be able to claim a refund via your credit card provider, or possibly your debit card."

Those stuck abroad should contact insurers, while those with package holidays reliant on Norse Atlantic flights should contact their tour operator, he added.

Norse Atlantic Airways was set up in 2021 as a low-cost long-haul carrier.

It entered the market as a successor to Norwegian, which withdrew from long haul routes as a result of the Covid pandemic.

But it has struggled to make money, and its problems worsened this year, as fuel prices rocketed due to the war in Iran.

Unlike many other European carriers, Norse Atlantic does not hedge its fuel bills by buying supplies in advance at fixed prices.

This left it fully exposed when prices soared, with the cost of fuel roughly doubling at one point. Prices remain significantly higher than they were before the conflict began.

In the first half of the year Norse Atlantic made a loss of $94.6m.

In a statement to the Oslo Stock Exchange on Wednesday, the airline said its financial situation was critical, and it needed to find short term funding to continue its operations.

After suspending flights, the company said it was in discussions with investors regarding a possible takeover that "would include a financing solution".

However, it said if short term funding could not be found quickly, "it is the Board's intention to file for bankruptcy".

Norse Atlantic had been looking for a buyer since July.

Its potential collapse follows the failure of Spirit Airlines in May. The US-based low cost carrier was another airline left exposed when jet fuel prices soared, as US airlines typically do not hedge their purchases.

If Norse Atlantic were to fold, it would be another major setback for the low-cost long-haul model, which has typically proved popular with passengers but difficult to sustain financially, especially on transatlantic routes.

Additional reporting by Rozina Sini

FinanceTab.title: Drivers over 70 face eye tests every three years under new plans
FinanceTab.text:
Over-70s will have to take eye tests every three years or face losing their driving licence under new road safety plans.

Mandatory eyesight tests are part of the Department for Transport's (DfT) road safety strategy, expected within weeks.

Around 6.5 million over-70s hold drivers' licences, with 1.6 million of those aged 80 or over.

To drive legally in the UK, you must be able to read a standard number plate from 20 metres away, wearing glasses or contact lenses if required.

Government sources told the BBC ministers will recommend over-70s be made to regularly prove their eyesight meets the minimum standards. Those who do not, or who fail to meet the minimum standard face losing their licence.

The change follows a consultation which launched early last year, set to recommend a shake-up of the rules for older drivers.

Under the current rules, over 70s have to renew their licence every three years, but only have to self-certify that their sight.

Dennis Reed, of campaign group Silver Voices, which represents older people, said it was "discriminatory to just pick an age out of the hat and say 'everybody over 70 has to go through this, but nobody else does'".

But he said the group is not opposed in principle to regular eye tests for older drivers.

FinanceTab.title: New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause
FinanceTab.text:
The government and the EU have published the texts of two treaties agreed last week as part of a post-Brexit reset.

The treaties were published on Thursday afternoon, alongside legislation designed to enact the bulk of the deal.

The deal covering food exports has a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party ended the agreement, they would have to pay "reasonable and proportionate costs" to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which will be significantly scaled back as part of the new deal.

Opposition leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would scrap the deal while Reform UK's Nigel Farage has suggested he would refuse to pay.

The Brexit reset deal has already sparked debate about its benefits, its costs, and a wider discussion on the future of the UK-EU relationship.

The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

Two of the three legal texts were released on Thursday, covering the food trade and emissions trading scheme deals, alongside the government's cost-cutting bill to enact the deal.

A new assessment of the impact of the deal on different sectors and regions of the country was also released.

Under the deal, food exporters will be significant beneficiaries from the scrapping of considerable red tape and checks, and dismantling of border facilities. An internal analysis forecasts a 16% boost the export of major agricultural commodities.

The industry and government hope the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers, but there may be no clear visible impact at the checkout.

Privately, industry insiders told the BBC earlier this week that there are too many moving parts in the world economy, in particular the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

Regarding the fine detail in the text of one of the treaties relating to the 10-year termination clause, European affairs minister Hamish Falconer said: "The Cutting Costs Bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements."

"It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes, and make doing business with our largest trading partner cheaper and easier."

A plan to link British and European emissions trading schemes will see more coverage across the UK's aviation and maritime industries.

The treaty text also contains finer detail of how the UK will observe, shape but not vote on relevant EU rules. The UK will be invited to attend European Commission meetings and expert groups as an observer, as well as taking part in emergency food security planning.

However, the UK will not be given voting rights.

Plans to use secondary legislation, including granting direct so-called "Henry VIII powers" to ministers to align UK and EU laws, are detailed in the legislation.

Such powers will enable ministers to make changes to bills with less Parliamentary scrutiny.

Outlining the agreement with the EU to MPs earlier this week, the prime minister said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything".

Andy Burnham also said it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.

Several former prime ministers have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate. Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour.

Badenoch said Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015".

FinanceTab.title: Nvidia value climbs by almost $1tn and tech stocks rally after Jensen Huang returns
FinanceTab.text:
Nvidia's market value rose by nearly $1 trillion as its share price skyrocketed after the tech firm reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive with immediate effect.

His shock reinstatement comes less than two weeks after Huang resigned after admitting an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy, a period in which shares in the chipmaker have also fallen significantly.

Nvidia shares rose by more than 31% which also lifted stock markets, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq climbing by 6.5% and the S&P 500 also rose 4.75%.

Tech stocks more broadly have also rallied following large falls on Friday, with much of the rally starting in pre-market trading before Huang's return was announced.

Other chipmakers experienced large increases following Monday's announcement from the Nvidia board. Shares in Micron Technology jumped 19%, while AMD shares rose nearly 7%.

Tesla shares also lept up by nearly 11.5%, while other tech gains were more muted by comparison: Amazon shares were up nearly 3.5%, and Apple and Microsoft rose by less than 2%.

While the surge in Nvidia shares was large and drove its market value back towards $4tn, the firm's share price remains about 21% down from a month ago.

A sharp drop occurred on 4 November, after the Democrat's midterm election victory sparked fears of tougher AI regulation to come led to a broad tech stock sell-off.

On Friday alone, Nvidia shares fell by 13.7% as tech stocks more broadly fell, and as Reuters reported - unconfirmed by the BBC - that the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) over its accounting practices.

Nvidia is a key firm at the core of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, with the chips it makes central to the industry.

Nvidia's board of directors voted unanimously to reinstate the firm's co-founder following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him, the company said - but US President Donald Trump has claimed he "convinced" the board to reinstate Huang.

Kathleen Brooks, research director at brokerage firm XTB, said Huang's return showed Huang was the "godfather" of AI, and "has a talismanic influence over the sector".

"Barely two weeks ago this man was ousted from the company that he founded due to serious misconduct and potential national security issues," she said.

"Even though Huang did not hold special voting shares on the board, Nvidia's directors cannot see a future for the company without him."

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said Huang's reinstatement was an astonishing about-turn for Nvidia, particularly given reports of an as-yet unconfirmed SEC investigation.

"This is the biggest corporate U-turn in living memory. To go from being embroiled in a spy scandal to being reinstated as the head of one of the world's most valuable companies in less than a fortnight is nothing short of remarkable," he said.

"Today's stock market rebound represents a massive sigh of relief by investors. However, one cannot rule out a more conservative approach by Huang going forward.

"His every move will be scrutinised by the market, and he may wish to tread more carefully to protect his integrity and ensure that Nvidia is being run responsibly."

Politicians are also demanding greater scrutiny.

Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said Huang's reinstatement "reportedly at the encouragement of Trump Administration officials and without any apparent accounting or response to the risks to our national security, demands an explanation."

She added: "What is abundantly clear is that the AI industry requires guardrails and oversight."

FinanceTab.title: China reserves right to take ‘necessary measures’ after Trump’s new tariff proposals
FinanceTab.text:
Beijing has said it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” after Donald Trump’s administration proposed new tariffs on goods from China and other major trading partners, triggering a global backlash.

Among the suggested levies on 14 major trading partners announced on Wednesday, China is potentially facing one of the biggest hits. It would face the highest capped rate of 20%, which in some cases will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%.

“China urges the United States to correct its erroneous practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation,” the Chinese commerce ministry spokesman, He Yadong, said at a regular briefing. “China will closely monitor developments and reserves the right to take necessary measures to firmly defend its legitimate rights and interests.”

Brazil was also singled out in the announcement after trade talks stalled.

Brazil’s government said on Wednesday that “Brazil will not yield to this type of threat”, adding in its statement that the “unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the framework of the ongoing bilateral negotiating process”.

It voiced particular indignation at US proposals for higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a change that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.

It added that Brazil would continue to negotiate “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products”.

The Trump administration said that the new tariffs would be consistent with trade deals that the US reached last year with dozens of countries. They are being imposed under a law that allowed the president to target countries the US had found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices. Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative, told CNBC that many US trading partners had adopted “market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America’s manufacturing base”.

The Trump administration’s new tariff rates would be capped at lower ​levels ‌agreed under ​trade deals ​that have already been concluded or remain under negotiation.

The administration will seek feedback from affected industries and hold a hearing on 25 January, suggesting the final duties won’t take effect until February or March.

Trump met his counterpart, Xi Jinping, in Shenzhen last week but the escalation in tariffs will not be a surprise to China, Dan Wang, a director on Eurasia Group’s China team, told AFP news agency.

The US and China last year reached a trade truce but that is set to expire on 10 January 2027. Trump and Xi are expected to meet again in Miami on the sidelines of the G20 in December.

“It has become a pattern before every major top leader summit,” Wang said, adding that she did not think the new measures would derail relations between Washington and Beijing.

“Xi has a high incentive to keep bilateral relations stable leading up to the 21st (Communist) party congress in October 2027,”Wang said.

A spokesperson for China’s embassy in Washington rejected allegations that China was ‌a source of ⁠excess capacity.

“The so-called issue of ‘industrial overcapacity’ does not really exist and should not be used as a pretext for political manipulation,” the spokesperson said, urging the two sides to jointly deliver on agreements secured between Trump andd Xi.

Earlier, China’s foreign ministry restated its opposition while calling for the US to resolve the issue through dialogue. “A tariff war or a trade war serves no party’s interests,” said the spokesperson Guo Jiakun.

Greer told CNBC that the administration was proposing a “broad exemption” for $30bn worth of Chinese goods in line with the deal. “We’ve talked to our trading partners about this – they know what we’re proposing,” Greer said. “I think a lot of this is baked in.”

Some US analysts criticised the duties as too weak to change China’s trade practices.

China “is a bigger source of excess production than the rest of the world combined”, said Derek Scissors, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. Yet Wednesday’s proposal “barely raises existing tariffs on China and will make no difference to the country’s trade behaviour.”

The EU said it rejected the premise of new tariffs and expected the US to stick by a deal struck last year. “The EU and the US share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action,” said the European Commission spokesperson Olof Gill.

Vietnam’s trade ministry said it was ⁠working with the US to complete its trade deal as soon ⁠as possible and would coordinate with relevant US agencies.

It added it was “preparing ​and submitting ​rebuttal comments on the ​preliminary findings as well as on inaccurate submissions ​and allegations ‌made by ​interested ​parties”.

In response to the US announcement, the Indian government denied it had any structural excess capacity in ⁠any sector, ⁠adding that it remained committed to an early conclusion of ⁠a trade deal between the two countries. Greer has said the tariff ⁠on Indian imports would be capped at 17% if a trade deal was struck.

Taiwan was also earmarked for new tariffs but Taipei on Thursday said it was confident it would keep its existing ⁠15% tariff rate.

Taipei and Washington signed trade deals in January and February of ‌this year, which secured preferential treatment for semiconductors and other tech products that account for ​more than 70% of Taiwan’s exports to the US.

Other countries and regions affected by the new tariffs include Bangladesh, ‌Cambodia, the EU, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland and Thailand.

Tokyo’s top government spokesperson, Minoru Kihara, said it was “regrettable that a proposed measure targeting Japan has been announced”.

Singapore’s government said it was “very disappointed” with the proposals and denied it was protecting its domestic market or subsidising manufacturing.

Trump’s latest round of tariffs may be here to stay despite the Democrats’ electoral sweep in the US midterms. Some Democrats will probably support some of the tariffs, particularly on China. Trump can veto any legislation that seeks to overturn the import taxes.

However, the Democratic senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will take over the finance committee next year, said he would “use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariffs chaos”.

He added: “This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs. Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution.”

With Associated Press and Reuters

FinanceTab.title: Judge blocks Brendan Carr-led FCC from taking any further action against ABC’s licenses
FinanceTab.text:
The federal judge Loren L AliKhan on Wednesday granted a preliminary injunction blocking the Brendan Carr-led Federal Communications Commission (FCC) from taking any action curbing ABC’s ability to renew its broadcast licenses, after the network sued the agency in August over an unusual demand to apply early to renew the eight local licenses for stations it owns.

The FCC claimed that the early renewal process was necessary to procure documents related to an ongoing Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) investigation, but the network countered that it was being punished for editorial coverage that was deemed critical of the Trump administration. The FCC’s order came after Donald Trump and the first lady, Melania Trump, criticized ABC for a comment made by the late night host Jimmy Kimmel.

At a hearing early last month, AliKhan seemed skeptical of the FCC’s reasoning for the early renewal order.

In her ruling, the judge said that ABC is “likely to succeed on their first amendment claim” of retaliation.

In addition to granting ABC’s request for a preliminary injunction, the judge denied the FCC’s request to dismiss the case. But she also denied ABC’s request to prevent the FCC from taking “any actions, formal or informal, to coerce or threaten plaintiffs with sanctions in an effort to alter their exercise of editorial discretion”.

In her ruling, the judge acknowledged the seriousness of the possible penalties facing ABC – and the chilling effect produced by an early license renewal order on a news organization’s first amendment rights. “Given the extreme, indeed existential, nature of the possible penalty Plaintiffs face – loss of their broadcast licenses – the court concludes that early license renewal proceedings create a risk sufficient to chill a broadcaster of ordinary firmness,” she wrote. “Any broadcaster of ordinary firmness – wealthy or not – would not hesitate to think twice if faced with such an existential threat to its business.”

The judge highlighted Trump’s long-standing animus against ABC as a clear factor in the FCC’s actions. “Starting with expressions of hostility, President Trump has set his sights on Plaintiff ABC for several years now,” she wrote, adding that the chairperson, Brendan Carr, “has taken President Trump’s rhetoric as his marching orders”.

As for the timing of the early renewal order request, coming soon after Trump’s criticism of Kimmel, the judge wrote: “Against the backdrop of President Trump and Chairman Carr’s call-and-response, it is no coincidence that President Trump criticized Mr. Kimmel’s skit on social media and the very next day Defendants initiated the early license renewal proceedings.”

The judge also noted the odd timing of the early renewal order, coming more than a year after the FCC began investigating ABC. And she acknowledged as credible the network’s concern that the agency’s license review process could run indefinitely.

“The existence of other mechanisms to solicit public input, coupled with the untenable timeline, casts serious doubt on the argument that Defendants are using the early license renewal proceedings to enhance public participation,” she wrote. “All told, the ‘significant mismatch’ between Defendants’ decision to order the proceedings when they did and their stated rationale for doing so presents an air of pretext the court will not ignore.”

In a statement, an ABC News spokesperson said: “Today’s decision is an important victory for the First Amendment. We thank the court for its careful consideration.”

Anna M Gomez, the lone FCC commissioner appointed by a Democratic president, also celebrated the judge’s ruling. “This decision shows that this FCC is a paper tiger whose threats crumble when challenged by those willing to defend their rights,” she said in a statement. “For nearly two years, the agency has weaponized its licensing authority to retaliate against broadcasters for exercising their right to free expression, and now a federal court has stepped in to put a check on that conduct. That brings badly needed accountability to a Commission and an administration that have politicized the machinery of government in a sustained campaign of censorship and control. Every broadcaster facing this pressure should take note and choose courage over capitulation because, as I’ve said from the beginning, the First Amendment is on their side.”

“While we appreciate the district court denying in part Disney’s request for preliminary injunctive relief, the portion of the decision granting Disney’s motion is wrong on the facts and wrong on the law – as controlling Supreme Court precedent makes clear,” a FCC spokesperson said in a statement. “The FCC looks forward to prevailing in full on this matter. We will continue to use our lawful authority to hold broadcasters accountable to their public interest obligations.”

FinanceTab.title: US inflation hits highest since May after prices climb 3.8% over the last year
FinanceTab.text:
The sell-off in US tech stocks continued on Wednesday as investors reacted to continued concern over the AI trade and fresh data that showed inflation jumped in October.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq index was down over 4% on Wednesday morning, while the S&P 500 had lost over 2.5% and the Dow had dropped about 2%. By the end of the day the tech-heavy index was down 0.6%, the S&P had lost 0.25% and the Dow managed a small gain of 0.33%.

After a rally upon the return of CEO Jensen Huang, Nvidia was down 5% at market’s closing on Tuesday and fell another 4% on Wednesday.

Anthropic shares rose 1% to end the day at $82.79, marginally lower than the $83-a-share price it was listed for during its blockbuster IPO last week.

New data released on Wednesday had shown consumer prices rose an annualized 3.8% in October, the highest rate since May.

This is the last inflation reading before a crucial US Federal Reserve board meeting next month, in which officials are largely expected to hike interest rates for the second time this year. The Fed has set a target inflation rate of 2%, a level not seen since February 2021. Higher interest rates make it more expensive to borrow money, slowing price increases, and raising the price of loans like mortgages and student debt.

Prices rose 0.3% from September to October amid soaring energy prices, according to the personal consumption expenditure index, the Fed’s preferred inflation measure from the commerce department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis.

The data comes after the Bureau of Labor Statistics separately reported prices climbed 0.4% from September to October, higher than economists had anticipated.

Energy prices, including gas prices at the pump, have cooled, going from a high of $4.41 a gallon in early October to $3.61 a gallon by mid-November, according to AAA.

Though Fed officials held rates steady at the last board meeting in late October, minutes from the meeting showed that some expressed concern about inflation’s stickiness.

“A few of them warned that further delay risked allowing high inflation to become entrenched or necessitating a larger and more disruptive tightening later,” the minutes said.

The move would come at a tumultuous time for the US economy. A new survey from the Conference Board released on Tuesday showed consumer confidence had ticked up in November to its highest level since January 2025, probably driven by the shake-up from the midterm elections.

SportsTab.title: Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua: How heavyweight rivals changed British boxing forever
SportsTab.text:
They have conquered the world, filled stadiums and transformed British boxing.

Now, after more than a decade of lingering tension and endless debate, Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua are finally preparing to share a ring.

They are from different worlds, with contrasting personalities and wildly different journeys to the summit of heavyweight boxing.

Fury is the unpredictable showman who dethroned a seemingly unbeatable champion. Joshua is the Olympic golden boy who became a global superstar.

Who is better? Who has achieved more? The arguments have raged in pubs, boxing gyms and across social media.

We may soon get our answer, but whatever happens when the first bell sounds in Cardiff in the early hours of 12 December, their greatest achievement may already be secure.

Together, Joshua and Fury have taken British heavyweight boxing to new heights, attracting wider audiences and inspiring the next generation.

Britain had produced heavyweight champions before, but for years many of the division's biggest fights took place overseas.

Lennox Lewis fought some of his defining bouts in Las Vegas and Memphis. Challengers travelled to Germany when the Klitschko brothers reigned.

In November 2015, Fury outpointed Wladimir Klitschko in Dusseldorf. Less than five months later, Joshua knocked out Charles Martin at London's O2 Arena to win his first world title in his 16th professional fight.

"Bosh, that's it. The revolution starts in that six-month period," said BBC Radio 5 Live boxing pundit Steve Bunce, who was interviewed for the BBC documentary Rivals: Fury v Joshua.

Joshua's former trainer Rob McCracken saw an early sign of his appeal in Birmingham, where a show sold out with Joshua on the undercard.

"I'm from Birmingham, and it's hard to get a big crowd that sort of size," McCracken says. Promoters soon realised Joshua was bringing in a different audience and could sell tickets almost instantly.

By 2017, Joshua was fighting in front of 90,000 fans at Wembley Stadium, where he stopped Klitschko, while Fury's trilogy with Deontay Wilder made him a box-office draw in the USA.

"The two of them have been in eight massive stadium fights over an eight-year period," Bunce says. "That's reshaping British boxing history."

Yet for all the domestic ground they broke, both men eventually helped export the division's biggest nights back overseas - trading British stadiums for Saudi Arabian paydays, with even this Cardiff homecoming bankrolled by Turki Alalshikh's 'Riyadh Season' and timed for an American streaming audience.

Fury and Joshua's reach extended beyond boxing. Joshua became a familiar face on chat shows, while Fury stepped into a WWE ring and welcomed Netflix cameras into his home.

Derek Chisora, who lost three times to Fury, could see that wider appeal in the crowd on fight night.

"You've got a guy who's running a hedge fund for £2.5bn having a drink with a guy who works for the local council," Chisora says.

Crossover contests - both faced former UFC champion Francis Ngannou, while Joshua fought YouTuber Jake Paul - reflected a sport increasingly blending competition with entertainment. But a lot of boxing fans viewed those fights as lucrative, low-risk detours that stalled the division.

Even so, that mainstream visibility turned Fury and Joshua into household names - and sustains Britain as a major centre of the division for another generation.

Today, a new wave of British heavyweights - Daniel Dubois, Fabio Wardley and Moses Itauma - are stepping into a landscape Joshua and Fury helped create.

Seven years after Joshua stopped Klitschko at Wembley, Dubois beat Joshua on the same ground. "Two legends of the sport," Dubois says. "What they've done for the sport in the last few years has been great."

Highly rated British prospect Leo Atang was 10 when he watched Joshua beat Klitschko on television at home in York and decided to give boxing a go. Seven years later, he won gold at the World Under-19 Championships.

Wardley remembers Fury's win in Dusseldorf as the night that "re-sparked a lot of people's love for boxing".

Yet for all Fury and Joshua have achieved, the one question has followed them both throughout their careers is: what would happen if they met in the ring?

After failed negotiations, lost titles and shifting circumstances, some believe their bout is arriving too late. Chisora describes it as "getting the last drink in the barrel".

For years, promotional politics, rival broadcast deals, and mutual risk aversion kept both camps protecting their commercial brands rather than risking undefeated records.

In the time it took to make the fight, both men lost twice to Oleksandr Usyk and Joshua was beaten by Andy Ruiz Jr and Dubois.

Fury's father John Fury did not even want the fight to take place.

"Both men are bigger than boxing, both men [are] bigger than the event. Leave them, they're both multi-millionaires. They don't need to fight," he says.

But former world champion Natasha Jonas believes legacy ultimately comes down to what fighters feel they have achieved.

"Legacies are a huge thing. Once you walk away, you want to be happy and satisfied with what you've done and what you've left behind," she says.

The reality is that - barring a late withdrawal - Fury and Joshua will put their reputations on the line in front of 80,000 fans in Cardiff.

But, whether their rivalry is settled in 12 rounds or a single punch, Fury and Joshua's wider legacy has been built over more than a decade of filling stadiums, drawing new audiences and making British heavyweight boxing a global attraction.

SportsTab.title: Sandpapergate: Cricket Australia outlines terms of reference for independent hearing into scandal
SportsTab.text:
Cricket Australia's fresh independent probe into the sandpapergate scandal has been widened to include the 2017-18 Ashes series against England.

The terms of reference for the independent forum have been published and the scope will include "ball-management practices in the Australian men's team during the 2017–18 season", which includes the Ashes series Australia won 4-0.

Also included are all four Tests of the subsequent South Africa tour and the investigation which followed when the ball-tampering scandal emerged.

Cricket Australia has pledged to publish the full independent report and recommendations within 30 days of receiving them.

All those involved in Australia's 2018 tour of South Africa will be invited to speak to the independent forum, though none will have to do so and no retrospective sanctions will be handed out.

The scandal was reignited by the release of former batter Usman Khawaja's autobiography. In it, Khawaja claimed the entire team knew about ball-tampering in the third Test of their series against South Africa in Cape Town.

The four frontline bowlers in that 2018 team - Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc, Nathan Lyon and current Test captain Pat Cummins - have always denied knowledge of the plan to use sandpaper on the ball.

Cummins has called Khawaja's recollection of events "nonsense".

However, former team-mates David Warner and Cameron Bancroft - two of three players who were banned for their part in the scandal, alongside Steve Smith - have backed Khawaja's version of events.

"All participants in Australia's 2018 tour of South Africa, including players and support staff, will be invited to take part in the Independent Forum, as will CA management and directors at that time," Cricket Australia said.

"While all involved will be encouraged to participate, there will be no compulsion to do so. All materials supplied will be treated as confidential unless otherwise stated by the participant and no sanctions will be retrospectively applied.

"Participants can choose to attend the Independent Forum in person, online and/or provide information via written accounts or through relevant documents and materials."

The forum will be open for six weeks.

"This is an opportunity to provide their accounts in a safe environment and to provide the CA Board with relevant information including about the events of that tour and resultant investigation," CA chair David Boon said.

"We are acutely aware of the enormous toll the renewed focus on this tour eight years ago has had on those involved and their welfare remains our main priority.

"This forum is the best opportunity for people to speak and be heard, and for CA to listen and learn.

"Publishing the report in full is part of our commitment to transparency, and to be open with cricket fans about what we learn.

"It is also very important to understand that it will not seek to sanction or recriminate."

SportsTab.title: Manchester City charges: Owners should be forced to sell, say Premier League rivals
SportsTab.text:
Manchester City's owners must be forced to sell up as punishment for breaking financial rules, senior figures at Premier League clubs have told BBC Sport.

This week, the chair of the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) David Kogan claimed he has the "stomach" to take action against City, who deny wrongdoing and have appealed.

The IFR has the power to remove directors of a club if they are deemed unsuitable, and even force a sale in the most serious cases.

Now, executives at three top-flight rivals have told the BBC that they believe this is the appropriate punishment for City, who were found guilty of breaching Premier League financial regulations rules between 2009 and 2018, and failing to co-operate with an investigation.

The independent commission has yet to decide on a sanction that could range from a fine, to a points deduction, the stripping of past titles, or even expulsion from the league.

But speaking on condition of anonymity, one executive claimed they are among a group of clubs who feel that City's punishment will be irrelevant unless the owners are also forced to sell. They added that anything less will make them question why they are funding the regulator through a levy.

In comments that reveal the level of anger felt by some of City's rivals, another claimed the rule breaches had undermined the league's credibility, and that they would not be able to draw a line under the scandal and move on if the owners were allowed to stay. The club were found guilty of inflating revenues and disguising losses by £900m through "sham" commercial arrangements.

Manchester City's owners are Abu Dhabi United Group - a private investment company belonging to United Arab Emirates vice-president and deputy Prime Minister Sheikh Mansour.

The executive who spoke anonymously said that clubs had been asked by the Premier League to refrain from publicly revealing their views on sanctions, and let the process run its course, although some are said to have privately made their opinions clear to IFR officials. They acknowledged that some clubs were less opinionated about a punishment.

Other clubs the BBC approached declined to comment, or said they were willing for the independent commission panel and IFR to reach their own conclusions following the publication of the commission's ruling in September.

But the fact that some clubs want the unprecedented sanction of a forced sale will put pressure on Kogan to mete out the harshest penalty possible in what is being seen as a defining test of the watchdog just over a year after it was established.

It also comes amid mounting questions over whether wider UAE trade and investment in UK projects could be impacted by such a move. In September, Prime Minister Andy Burnham was criticised for saying he would be "really concerned" if the scandal led to City's owners selling the club, adding that "they have been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester".

When approached, the IFR declined to comment. But Kogan has consistently said that the IFR will not be influenced by any political pressure.

Earlier this week he told a parliamentary committee that the watchdog would not be afraid to investigate City's hierarchy and take action, depending on the outcome of the appeal.

"Forget the name of the club, forget the size of the club, forget the scale of the issue. We cannot simply ignore our statutory duties in relation to a club because it happens to be of a certain size," Kogan said.

"We absolutely will have to take the appropriate action as laid out in the legislation, depending on the circumstances as they come to us, which are the evidence that's been presented and collated by the independent commission of the Premier League and by any judgement that takes place on that evidence through an appeal.

"But in one sense, the evidence has already been judged by those cases having been found guilty, so we will absolutely have the stomach to do so... assuming those circumstances are triggered, if we don't act, what is the purpose of having a football regulator?"

SportsTab.title: Bournemouth 'dreaming' of winning Europa League after beating Celta Vigo
SportsTab.text:
Bournemouth are dreaming of winning the Europa League after staging a 10-man fightback to join a select band of teams to win their first five European games.

The Cherries trailed 1-0 to Iago Aspas' goal at Celta Vigo, and then went down to 10 men midway through the first half when Bafode Diakite was sent off.

But second-half goals from Alvaro Rodriguez and Rayan gave the Cherries a 10th consecutive win in all competitions, extending their club record run.

Bournemouth are only the third side to win each of their first five European matches (excluding qualifiers and including the Inter-Cities Fairs Cup), after Nuremberg in 1961-62 and Ararat in 1972-73.

They top this season's table as the only club to win five out of five - and are closing in on a top-eight spot, which would mean they skip a play-off round and go straight into the last 16.

Some fans have told the BBC they have already booked hotels in Frankfurt for the final on 26 May.

As supporters sang about reaching that game, midfielder Alex Scott was asked for his thoughts on TNT Sports.

"Of course that's our dream. When you grow up wanting to be a footballer you dream of winning trophies," Scott said.

"Where this club has come from to where it is now, full credit to everyone who has built it.

"For players, it's a dream to be on the pitch playing for this club. We have still got wins to get to qualify into the top eight, and from there all focus is on pushing forward and hopefully we can go on and win it."

The Cherries are in unprecedented times, with their biggest trophy to date being when they won the second-tier Championship in 2014-15.

In terms of cups, they won the 1983–84 Associate Members' Cup - which later became the EFL Trophy.

Head coach Marco Rose, who replaced Andoni Iraola in the summer, said: "It's always allowed to dream.

"If you get a competition like this you want to achieve the best possible thing. We know it's far away to go. Many games. Now it's about getting into the top eight to avoid more games and then we can see step by step."

As well as just winning their games, Bournemouth are firing in the goals. They have netted at least twice in each match during this 10-game winning run.

And they are the first side to score at least twice in each of their first five matches in Europe since Queens Park Rangers in 1976.

The win on Thursday was made even more impressive by the fact they contested 75% of the game with 10 men.

It came days after Manchester United seemed to implode after an early red card against Liverpool, losing 4-0.

Former England manager Glenn Hoddle said on TNT: "They have deserved this result. They've played beautifully with 10 men - probably as good as I've seen a team play defensively and with the ball.

"I've not seen a team go down to 10 men for so long and dictate a game and deserve to win the game. They were absolutely brilliant."

Cherries boss Rose told BBC Radio Solent: "What a team, what a spirit, what an energy.

"I said to Ty [Tyler Adams] sometimes it's not about tactics and formations and stuff like this. [David] Brooks did a great job when we got one player less - he played right defender like he played it for 10 years. We changed in the right moment. Everyone did his job on a really high level.

"We were just relentless and we never stopped to believe in this win and that's why big, big, big congratulations to the team.

"You feel if you're one player down that it's a difficult night, but to handle a difficult night like this, it just shows the character of the team and of the whole group."

The coach's belief in what they are doing filters through to the players.

Amine Adli, who set up the equaliser, told the BBC: "At half-time, everyone still believed we can turn the game in our way and this is what happened.

"Everyone was like 'guys we can make it, we have to believe. If we score the game can change.'"

Earlier this month, the attacking midfielder said he saw a lot of similarities to the Bayer Leverkusen team he was part of in 2023-24.

That is not a bad comparison, considering they went unbeaten to win the domestic double, as well as reaching the Europa League final.

So who can blame the Cherries for dreaming?

SportsTab.title: Phil Taylor: 16-time world champion and Adrian Lewis lose all five matches in return at pairs tournament
SportsTab.text:
Phil Taylor and his England team-mate Adrian Lewis lost all five matches as the pair returned to darts action together at the MODUS Super Series International Pairs tournament.

Taylor, a 16-time world champion, retired from senior-level darts in 2018, while Lewis has not competed on the PDC tour since 2023.

They signed for the tournament in Portsmouth after Taylor was tempted back by the prospect of playing alongside his long-term friend.

The 66-year-old landed his first dart at a double as he checked out on 84 but the duo went on to lose their opening match 4-3 against Scotland's John Henderson and Robert Thornton.

They subsequently suffered successive defeats to pairs from Sweden, Switzerland, Germany and Denmark.

The pair finished the night bottom of Group C, but will return to action on Friday for a second round-robin phase.

Taylor had not played competitively since the 2024 edition of World Seniors Darts Championship and was adamant the south-coast competition will be his last appearance at the tournament.

Speaking prior to his first match, he told Talksport, external: "This is the final time. It's got to be now. I've got all the things in my life now that I'm enjoying.

"I understand what Adrian's saying about travelling and being away. He's got a young family still, where my family have grown up, but I've still got grandkids.

"One stops and then another one begins again, life carries on. I enjoy being at home, that's the reason why I wouldn't be on the road again."

Taylor and two-time world champion Lewis, 41, won the World Cup of Darts four times together for England between 2012 and 2016.

Asked how his preparation for the tournament had gone, Taylor added: "For me, not very well, to be quite honest with you. I've lost it a little bit.

"Aidy, I know has been playing really well, so I'm going to be on his shoulders today. He's going to have to carry me a little bit."

SportsTab.title: 'Priceless' Duran proves 'the man' but is he papering over cracks at Celtic?
SportsTab.text:
"Duran is priceless for us at the moment".

It would be difficult for a football manager to muster up a higher compliment for one of his players - given he should know exactly how much he did cost - but Celtic boss Martin O'Neill was rightly effusive in his praise for Camilo Duran.

With 15 goals in 23 appearances, six assists, and another late European winner on Thursday, the Colombian was once again the main man for a struggling Celtic side.

His double against Besiktas breathed life into their Europa League campaign last time out, and his late leap to nod in the winner against Torreense kept it alive.

Duran, 24, started on the bench but was brought on with just over half an hour to go as O'Neill watched his side labour against a team currently 13th in the Portuguese second tier.

Celtic would still be searching for their first European win were it not for their summer arrival from Qarabag, whose goals have played a key part in keeping his team within touching distance of a play-off spot with three fixtures to play.

"He's taken on this mantle of being the man and he's been fantastic," said O'Neill, who started Duran on the bench. "We tried a similar approach against Besiktas.

"Sometimes by the time Duran gets subbed on, you could be behind. But I think that's the sign of a brilliant player, he'll do something.

"He's not a big guy but he's just a super footballer, a super, super footballer."

Duran's summer arrival was overshadowed when, just over a fortnight later, a club-record fee was paid to Bodo Glimt for another striker, Kasper Hogh.

While recent weeks have been dominated by debates over Duran or Hogh, the debate now seems settled, with the Colombian operating on a different level from his striking counterpart.

Anyone watching Celtic in Portugal would have watched Hogh find space a handful of times in the area, but repeatedly fail to find a team-mate or trouble the goalkeeper. Duran didn't need to be asked twice.

"I don't know how many touches he got, but he had the telling touch," James McFadden said on Sportsound post-match.

SportsTab.title: BBC Men's Footballer of the Year 2026: Cast your vote
SportsTab.text:
Voting remains open for the BBC Men's Footballer of the Year 2026 award, which will be presented at Sports Personality of the Year.

Fans from the UK can vote from the five-player shortlist of Jude Bellingham, Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe, Rodri and Lamine Yamal.

The vote closes on Friday, 27 November at 09:00 GMT.

The winner of the award - new for this year - will be presented during the live Sports Personality of the Year show on Sunday, 13 December.

Alex Kay-Jelski, Director of BBC Sport, said: "From the drama and excitement of the men's World Cup to the moments that have captivated fans across the domestic and international game, 2026 has given us so much to celebrate.

"Our inaugural BBC Men's Footballer of the Year award is about recognising the players who have made this year so special, inspired fans and left their mark on the game.

"It's a fantastic shortlist, and I can't wait to see who the public choose as our first-ever winner."

The shortlist was selected by an expert panel comprising former international players and some of the BBC's most respected football voices, bringing together a wealth of experience and insight from across the game.

The panel included Cesar Azpilicueta (Spain), Scott Brown (Scotland), Olivier Giroud (France), Shay Given (Republic of Ireland), Hassan Kachloul (Morocco), Lucas Leiva (Brazil), Benni McCarthy (South Africa), Alan Shearer, Ellen White (both England) and Ashley Williams (Wales).

SportsTab.title: Rishabh Pant: India star joins New Zealand club match under false name
SportsTab.text:
India wicketkeeper Rishabh Pant made a surprise appearance for a club team in Christchurch under the false name 'Stan Stan'.

Pant, 29, played for the Open House Swingers against The Chosen Ones and smashed 54 from 21 balls in a 16-run win.

His appearance came a day before India's second Test against New Zealand, which begins at the Hagley Oval at 22:00 GMT on Thursday.

Open House player Mohammad Safi told the New Zealand Herald that he had seen Pant on an electric bike in the city and approached him, saying that his team were a player short.

Safi also said that Pant was not immediately recognised by many on either side, and he turned up in a purple tracksuit and had to borrow kit.

New Zealand captain Tom Latham said Pant's appearance was "brilliant" and showed his "real character", while India bowling coach and former South Africa quick Morne Morkel said he "nearly fell off my chair" when he saw the footage that circulated on social media.

The first Test in Wellington ended in a high-scoring draw, where Pant scored 128 in India's only innings of 720-9.

Pant is regarded as one of the world's most entertaining cricketers, and has scored 3,853 runs in his 53 Tests at an average just shy of 45.

Of those to have scored more than 2,000 Test runs for India, only Virender Sehwag and Kapil Dev have a better strike-rate than Pant's 74.43.

SportsTab.title: Laura Freigang: Germany forward banned for missing drugs tests
SportsTab.text:
Germany international Laura Freigang has been suspended from football for 16 months over issues with three drugs tests.

The 28-year-old will miss the Women's World Cup next summer and is banned from all football activity until after 7 October 2027.

The 16-month suspension begins from the date of notification by the German Football Association (DFB), which took place in June.

The World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada), the National Anti-Doping Agency (Nada), DFB and Freigang reached a dispute resolution agreement.

The dispute said Entracht Frankfurt forward Freigang committed three reporting and/or testing failures between 11 March 2025 and 23 February 2026.

Freigang can return to training two months prior to the end of the suspension period but cannot play matches until after 7 October.

All personal records of appearances, goals, assists or other statistics from 23 February 2026 are nullified, though Frankfurt's results are unaffected.

This season Freigang has scored six goals and provided two assists in 11 starts in the Frauen-Bundesliga.

Since joining the club in 2020, the striker has scored 107 goals in 187 appearances and was in the Germany squad for October's friendly victories over Australia and Japan.

In a club statement, external, Franfurt said they will "begin discussions shortly to determine the terms of her future employment relationship".

Freigang's current contract is due to expire on 30 June 2027.

Frankfurt's director of women's football Katharina Kiel said: "The agreement now reached provides clarity and planning security in a process unprecedented for Eintracht Frankfurt - for us as a club, but above all for Laura.

"The way she and the team have handled the situation in recent months, and how Laura personally led by example with her performance on the pitch during a very difficult time, deserves the highest recognition.

"The identified shortcomings, despite the agreement to settle the dispute, have resulted in a suspension, which means the loss of a key player."

SportsTab.title: Aston Villa: Alejandro Garnacho already at a career crossroads at Villa Park
SportsTab.text:
Alejandro Garnacho's time at Aston Villa has been brief - and it already looks to be over.

The latest snub by Villa boss Unai Emery was the most damming of all, with the on-loan Chelsea winger left out of Tuesday's Champions League defeat at Galatasaray.

"The players who were here I think are the best players to be here with us," said Emery.

Villa could have had 12 substitutes in Istanbul but Emery chose just 11 - including two goalkeepers - as Garnacho stayed at home.

The plan was for the Argentina international's loan move to become permanent for £43m should certain criteria be met.

They are believed to be based on a number of appearances staff felt were so achievable the club were in little doubt he would become a Villa player.

But now there is doubt he will ever play for them again.

"First start after three months. Happy to be enjoying football again."

The post Garnacho wrote on social media after a pre-season game in July has - along with anything else related to Villa - been deleted from his account.

He has played just 34 minutes in the Premier League this season, and seven of Villa's 11 games ended without him getting on the pitch.

His last appearance - just a three-minute cameo - came in the 1-1 draw against Fulham on 31 October.

Including Saturday's 0-0 draw with Sunderland, Garnacho has been omitted from the past three matchday squads - a strong sign Emery has lost faith in him.

But he may have been fighting a losing battle from the off, having arrived at Villa unfit.

Sources have acknowledged the 22-year-old was not at the level required and were surprised how off the pace he was when he signed in July.

He initially trained on his own, and questions over the signing were already being asked, with eyebrows raised by some internally given his inconsistent form for both Chelsea and Manchester United.

Yet he had been on Villa's list of targets - albeit a long list - while he was at Stamford Bridge as Emery was keen to sign a pacy winger in the summer.

Garnacho's problems were compounded by a head injury suffered in Thailand in pre-season, and even a boot camp during the international break in September and October, and scoring in friendlies against Sevilla and Southampton have not helped.

One of the issues Villa have is there is no exit clause, and both teams would have to agree to end the season-long loan deal early.

This time last year, Emery had already decided not to sign Harvey Elliott permanently in a £30m deal, leaving the on-loan Liverpool midfielder in limbo for the rest of the season.

And it appears Emery has already come to the same conclusion with Garnacho.

With Villa unable to find a solution with Liverpool, Elliott wasted a precious year of his career. Those close to him recognise the damage last season did, playing just nine times after being named Player of the Tournament at the European Under-21 Championship in 2025.

He is now at Valencia and is yet to start in La Liga this season.

The risk of going on loan to Villa became a topic of conversation in the game because of Elliott's plight, with sources suggesting players would think twice about joining the club. Garnacho's situation only increases those concerns.

Three times in two seasons, Emery and Villa have signed a high-profile player on loan only for it to fail.

Jadon Sancho's expensive loan from Manchester United last season - Villa paying a guaranteed 80% of Sancho's wages of more than £200,000 a week - ended with him having made just nine Premier League starts and scoring once in 39 appearances, with 21 of those as a substitute.

Sancho may have played more than Elliott and Garnacho - and came off the bench in their Europa League final win - but what value did Villa really get?

Of course, Marcus Rashford and Marco Asensio enjoyed positive loan spells previously - Rashford returning to the England squad while at Villa - but they are exceptions to the rule.

Nicolo Zaniolo, Clement Lenglet and Axel Disasi have joined in recent years and barely merit footnotes, while Douglas Luiz's loan return last season did not prompt a return to the heights he had reached previously at Villa.

The club have constantly complained about financial restrictions with some justification, but questions can certainly be asked about the money spent on many of their signings.

The blunt truth is there is no clear path.

Teenager George Hemmings has just signed a new deal and has earned praise from Emery for understanding the way he wants his players to work.

Ibrahim Mbaye and Alysson are also ahead of Garnacho, leaving him well behind even before regulars John McGinn, Johan Manzambi and Emi Buendia are factored in.

There was interest from abroad in the summer, with Roma keen, and it seems increasingly unlikely we will see Garnacho at another Premier League club soon.

Fifa rules allow players to play for two clubs in a season - or three if they move to a team whose season overlaps like the MLS - meaning Garnacho could feature for another, unlike Elliott as he had already played for Liverpool and Villa.

Garnacho, whose character has not been called into question while at Villa, cost Chelsea £40m when he signed from Manchester United in 2025 but failed to make a consistent impression, with eight goals in 43 games. When he joined Chelsea he signed a contract until 2032.

Prior to that, United boss Ruben Amorim had told him to leave.

Now nothing, it seems, will persuade Emery that Garnacho is worth persevering with - leaving the winger's career continuing to drift.

SportsTab.title: EA adds AI-generated John Motson to FC 27 video game
SportsTab.text:
Football game EA Sports FC will feature the digitally recreated voice of the late commentator John Motson, Electronic Arts has exclusively told the BBC.

Motson, who died in 2023, was the main commentator for BBC Sport for decades - and performed the same role for the video game series during the 90s and 00s.

It is the first time the hit series, formerly known as Fifa, has featured a deceased commentator.

With the permission of his widow and his son, Motson's voice has been synthesised using a combination of old recording sessions and generative AI. It will become available in FC 27 on 26 November.

The legendary commentator died aged 77 in February 2023 - several months after the launch of ChatGPT and the massive growth of AI it set in train.

Fred Motson told the BBC it "means an awful lot" to have his dad's voice in EA Sports FC once again.

"I grew up with Fifa," he said. "I always used to tell my parents that I needed the latest console for Christmas because otherwise dad couldn't see how the game worked."

Electronic Arts, which was bought for $55bn (£42bn) in August, told the BBC it paid Motson's family for the rights to use his likeness and recreate his voice, but would not disclose the financial terms of the deal.

The BBC's lead football commentator Guy Mowbray said it was a "privilege" to be involved in the game, which he has provided commentary for since 2023.

"I think it's quite a nice, sort of non-scary use of AI," he said.

"We're in the business of nostalgia... I hear commentary not in my own voice, but in John's voice, because that's the voice I knew growing up.

"So I think it's nice that that legacy can be continued in this way."

John Motson was the first commentator for the series, appearing on games from Fifa 96 up to Fifa 2005. He later made a brief cameo in Fifa 19.

"While he completely understood when they went in a different direction, I think he really missed it after he left the game and it felt like a bit of an end of an era," his son said.

EA told the BBC the studio would not have included Motson in the game unless they had permission from his family.

"There was no way we would have moved forward with this in any way, shape or form if they weren't fully on board," said Mat Prior, senior game design director at EA Sports FC.

"At the outset we wanted to pay tribute to Motty as the commentator and as this emotional connection - he was the very first voice of our game - so we really wanted to do him justice and bring him back."

He explained that Motson's voice in the game was a combination of old lines he recorded over the years and AI - tech which he said was "the only way" to make it happen, as they don't have recordings of him talking about modern players like Bradley Barcola and Chloe Kelly.

Motson's son Fred said he believed his dad would have "absolutely" wanted to be involved in the game after his death.

"My dad was the least technological person in the world," he said. "Till his dying day, he had a typewriter on his desk.

"So I don't think he would have quite understood what the AI was doing technologically - but I think, on the other hand, he was always really keen to get involved in these kinds of projects."

But Peter Caulfield, founder of Save Our Voices Now which campaigns against AI voice cloning, expressed some disquiet about the project, and the fact Motson had been unable to consent to it.

"If someone has signed a deal allowing their likeness to be used after they die, I have no issue with that," he said.

"But in life or in death, unless you have specifically agreed to it, AI cloning of any kind should not be allowed.

"Being a family member shouldn't automatically give you that right either."

One of the main arguments against the use of generative AI in video games is that it can replace humans - something that EA was keen to argue against.

"From a gaming standpoint, it's something we've used for many years - like machine learning to help drive animation systems and so on and so forth," Prior said.

"It's not there to replace commentators in any way shape or form... there's certainly no future plans to replace anyone with AI."

Derek Rae, who has been a commentator in EA FC for several years, said the tech could make things easier, but he still spent a long time recording dialogue in studios.

"It's quite a lot of days in the course of a year," he said. "So it might be two or three times a month that we do it in season for the game, which is typically sort of November time through until May.

"The more creative things have to be done with the human voice because they have to have the personality, sometimes a little chuckle thrown in the middle of a sentence or a little idiosyncrasy," he said.

"But when it comes to the more normal features in a video game, for example, routine surnames like Smith and Jones and Brown, that's something that AI can probably accomplish quite easily."

TechnologyTab.title: Jensen Huang: How the Nvidia scandal exposed the risks of Asia's big AI bet
TechnologyTab.text:
Jensen Huang's extraordinary return as Nvidia's boss rocked not only its shares in New York but also sent shockwaves through the artificial intelligence (AI) industry around the world.

Those jolts were felt particularly in Asia as the saga highlighted the region's huge exposure to the technology.

Tech-heavy stock indexes in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan went on a rollercoaster ride this week. Markets soared after a near-trillion dollar surge in Nvidia's share price but then slumped as concerns about political and regulatory scrutiny hit investor confidence.

The chipmaker is a "symbolic bellwether" of the AI trade that is fast becoming key to places like South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore and Malaysia," says Dylan Loh, an international studies lecturer at Nanyang Technological University.

From chip manufacturing to data centres to foreign investments, AI has become a strategic priority for these economies - and they are now increasingly dependent on Nvidia's fortunes.

In Nvidia, the AI industry has the unrivalled power of cutting-edge chips and the financial clout that turned it into "the bank of AI". And in Huang, it has a high-profile evangelist.

That combination has put it at the heart of the AI ecosystem in more ways than one.

For one, Nvidia was able to grow rapidly by outsourcing chip production instead of having to spend heavily to build its own manufacturing plants.

It contracts out most of its production to Taiwanese chipmaking giant TSMC.

That means Taiwan is vulnerable to changes in AI tech demand, says Paul Cavey, founder of Taipei-based research firm East Asia Econ.

"The surge in [Taiwan's] real economic growth since 2024 has been because of the big increase in AI related exports".

Huang said earlier this year that Nvidia plans to invest around $150bn (£114.4bn) a year in Taiwan at a launch to celebrate the firm's planned headquarters on the island.

To a lesser extent, South Korea and Japan are also exposed to the industry, Cavey adds. They are among its suppliers of key components such as memory chips and testing equipment, with firms like Samsung and SK Hynix making the firm's processors.

On top of that, Nvidia is a financial backstop and major lender to companies in the AI supply chain.

It is difficult to overstate the role Nvidia, with Huang at its helm, has played in the region's AI industry. Nvidia's chips fill its data centres, power its AI models and feed the companies making cars and electronics.

"Asia isn't just a customer base for Nvidia. It is an indispensable engine of the company's AI dominance because of East Asia's semiconductor manufacturing and memory ecosystems," Loh says.

In the Asia-Pacific region, the data centre market, which is largely powered by Nvidia chips, is in the midst of an "unprecedented boom", according to property services firm CBRE, external. The volume of investment has been rising steadily in recent years to reach a record of $11.6bn (£8.85bn) in 2025.

In South East Asia, Singapore-based AI company Megaspeed had become the region's biggest buyer of Nvidia chips before it was accused of smuggling them to China. Megaspeed has said it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".

The US has said it intends to ban Megaspeed Ltd from doing business in the United States.

But in a timely example of the importance of AI to this region, Singapore this week further raised its growth forecast for this year as the technology boosts its economy.

The world's biggest tech firms - Google, Microsoft, Oracle - also plan to boost their spending on infrastructure in the region by roughly 60% this year, CBRE added.

The demand for neoclouds, which are specialised data centres which power AI, has also risen rapidly, it said.

For economies betting heavily on AI, Nvidia has become "hugely important", with vast sums being spent on its chips and factory activity increasingly dependent on its technology, Loh told the BBC.

In many economies, news of Huang's return to Nvidia was met with jubilation.

In Taiwan, where he was born and the home of "Jensanity", investors jokingly described his return as a "one man saves the village" story.

Social media and groups on messaging platform Line saw posts like "Old Huang is back," while some investors said "Daddy is back to save my life" and "the humanitarian corridor is open."

However, some said the episode should also prompt a closer look at how effective Taiwan has been in building a "non-China" semiconductor supply chain, and how risks from the industry's heavy reliance on Nvidia should be managed better.

Asia's technology industry has been under increasing pressure from the US in recent years. The administrations of both Joe Biden and Donald Trump have tightened rules on the export of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China.

Those efforts seem to have been renewed. Just last week, Washington announced new rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.

The latest move not only restricts the export of high-end chips to China, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train AI models.

This will hit South East Asian countries, which have invested billions in data centre infrastructure to cater to Chinese firms. Nvidia has already paused shipments to the region, according to the Financial Times, although it is unclear if this is only a temporary move while it figures out how to comply with the new export rules.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a BBC request for comment.

Then there is the growing bipartisan backlash against President Trump and Nvidia after he said he "made the deal" to "convince" the company‘s board to reinstate Huang.

Huang is also due to testify before Congress next week. And as Democrats prepare to take control of the US House and Senate in the New Year, Huang is likely to face further risks.

"Jensen's return may resolve the immediate leadership crisis, but it does not resolve the legal and political overhangs," said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist from Saxo Bank.

Investor concerns about the trillions of dollars being poured into AI and the pivotal role Nvidia plays in the industry were already sending tremors through global stock markets.

Some fear that while the company and its charismatic leader have been crucial in driving AI's growth that concentration of influence also poses a threat.

Especially now when it appears that Huang's future - which is still uncertain - could impact economies that are heavily exposed to the AI industry.

"I would say the President and White House would love to brush this over and say its fine but I believe Democrats in Congress will definitely be probing", Ray Wang, founder of San Francisco-based Constellation Research said.

"The story is not over yet... Jensen coming back is probably the biggest, baddest return ever. The question is what will happen next?"

Additional reporting by Benny Lu, BBC Chinese

TechnologyTab.title: Why there's a shortage of lift and escalator mechanics
TechnologyTab.text:
Some of them are angry. Nerves are frayed. Many of them are just relieved that he's here.

When a lift stops working in Chicago, frazzled building managers might get a visit from Jim Lembesis. For more than 47 years, Lembesis has repaired and upgraded lifts. He says he understands why staff and residents are so anxious to have things working again.

"They wait and they wait," says Lembesis, a field technician for Parkway Elevators. "There's a lot of frustration. Sometimes it's a repeat issue. It's a never-ending cycle, you know what I mean?"

The widely reported shortage of lift and escalator mechanics in the US, which is also a problem in many other countries, has got worse over time, he adds: "It's been like night and day compared to when I started."

Everyone needs a lift now and again. Some people depend on them – elderly residents of high-rise buildings, say, or wheelchair users.

Storm-damaged lifts in Hawaiian apartment blocks this year left some residents trapped, external in their homes for weeks. A lack of mechanics, and problems sourcing parts, were blamed for the repair delays.

In the US, the average salary for a lift mechanic, external is $110,000 (£83,000). And yet people in the industry say it is difficult to attract new workers.

Sure, says Lembesis, you do encounter some dangers in a job like this. There are risks of falling from a great height – or being electrocuted. Once, he was even hit on the head with an umbrella by an elderly lady after he rescued her from a stuck lift.

But there are so many skills to learn, and great camaraderie and knowledge-sharing among mechanics, he says. As one recruiter puts it, these technicians amaze people with their ability to fix things. They are like "wizards". The overall-clad shamans who know how to get modern life running again.

Nine times out of 10, the problem is with the doors, says Lembesis. These components repeatedly move back and forth. "People hit them with carts, and dirt and debris [falls into them]," says Lembesis. "[The doors] take the most beating."

Mechanics often keep various spare door parts in their vehicles, ready to use.

But technicians like Lembesis don't just have to get lifts working, they also have to verify the lifts are safe. He remembers one case, decades ago, getting called out to a burning building. His role was to ensure the lifts, which were being drenched with huge volumes of water, were still safe to use while firefighters tackled the blaze.

"I was there for 15 hours that night," he says. "Everyone, on the way out of the door, shook my hand."

Finding good lift technicians is "becoming more difficult" says Matt Hollinshead, president of the US National Association for Elevator Contractors. "We have a four-year apprenticeship," he says. That's the first hurdle. And many states require certification or licensing before you can work on lifts.

"We have a vast array of equipment that has to be maintained in the United States." Some lifts are 100-years-old. As time goes on, the technological knowledge required to repair them only grows.

Hollinshead says that weeks or months-long delays to lift repairs are not typically due to staff shortages but that, in such cases, it's likely that a particular part isn't readily available. Manufacturing a replacement hydraulic cylinder takes six to 12 weeks, he notes.

But the lack of technicians does mean that that building managers might have to wait days before someone can even diagnose what's wrong with a lift after it stops working.

Hollinshead says teaching the basics of the trade in high schools or technical schools could entice more people into the role.

Matt Allred, a recruiter and host of The Elevator Careers Podcast, emphasises the many skills that lift mechanics require. "You're a little bit of a wizard, right? You show up and if you can fix it – 'Wow!'."

He blames major lift companies, in part, for locking down maintenance contracts, making it difficult or impossible for third-party repairers to intervene when a lift fails.

Two large lift manufacturers approached by BBC News declined interviews. The chief executive of Otis, one of the firms, said in May that her company was struggling to hire enough staff, external to meet demand. The firm also states on its website, external that the shortage of lift mechanics affects "almost every part of the world".

However, a spokesman for Otis claimed its "US talent pipeline" was healthy, and declined an interview.

Everyone else who spoke to BBC News said hiring was challenging in the US. Allred was recently contacted by a major lift company and asked to help them find a technician. "I was surprised that a major company would reach out to a little recruiting shop," he says, suggesting that this reflects the extent of the labour shortage.

That shortage is also a problem in the UK. "It is bad and getting worse," says Dave Cooper, president of the Chartered Institution of Building Services Engineers, who is also chief executive of a lift and escalator engineering consultancy.

"We've known food delivery companies to refuse to deliver to flats above the ground floor because the lift is out of service."

Offering better tax breaks to companies that train lift mechanics could help ensure that plenty of workers continue to enter the industry, he adds.

Training to be a lift mechanic is "not a quick route to competency – and it requires people to stick at it for the long term" says Karen Slade, head of assessment at the Lift and Escalator Industry Association (Leia).

Continued investment in training and attracting new workers is "essential", according to Leia. There are currently 259 active lift and escalator apprentices in the UK, the body adds.

Back in Chicago, Lembesis is working with two younger mechanics who have been "really good", he says, so there's at least some hope for the future.

He stresses again how rewarding he finds his work. The people for whom he fixes lifts tend to be very appreciative.

"I love that. You get that reaction from the customers," he says. "Without them, you got nothing."

He says he understands why staff and residents are so...
