TechnologyTab.title: US approves SpaceX plan to send a million data satellites to space
TechnologyTab.text:
US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind.

The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, would "support America's booming super intelligence economy".

However, rival firm Amazon has criticised it as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan", while astronomers in the US said the move would "significantly undermine" the public's ability to study and observe the night sky.

There is increasing opposition to data centres on earth, including in the US where experts say they were a factor in the Republicans big losses in the midterm elections.

SpaceX believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities".

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth".

"This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said.

Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."

Under the FCC licence, deployment of the satellites must begin no later than November 2033. SpaceX will be required to have deployed 10% by November 2035, rising to 50% by November 2038.

The company has already said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year.

It is unclear whether a million satellites will indeed be launched or whether SpaceX has sought approval for a higher number than it will use.

Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles).

Starmind's satellites will communicate with Starlink's and then relay the data to Earth.

Speaking to the Today programme, on BBC Radio 4, Prof Sir Martin Sweeting, founder and executive chairman of Surrey Satellite Technology Ltd, said while the idea of data centres in space seemed "technically feasible", whether it "makes sense at scale yet" still needed to be analysed.

Being able to get the data from the network of satellites, he added, would depend on being able to use laser links from the ground to them.

"That has not yet been perfected to the level at which it would be able to support the huge amounts of data that are likely to be transferred backwards and forwards," he said.

Meanwhile, the American Astronomical Society (AAS) said it was "disheartened and dismayed" by the decision.

It said the proposed constellation would "significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities" as well as "the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky".

It noted that the constellation "involves larger (and therefore brighter) and more numerous objects", meaning the satellites would "be visible as extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky".

Jan Hasselman, a senior attorney at the non-profit group Earthjustice, said in a statement: "Drastically expanding satellites in space has a direct impact on people's everyday lives as well as the future of our planet."

TechnologyTab.title: Huawei found guilty of stealing US trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
TechnologyTab.text:
Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark case in the US.

In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.

Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation.

Huawei said, external the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis", adding that it would "take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests".

Jurors in a Brooklyn court found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, which included conspiracy to violate US sanctions.

However, the jury declined to convict Huawei of the racketeering conspiracy charge, which required members to find the firm acted like a criminal enterprise.

Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019, after the dramatic arrest in late 2018 of senior executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada.

Meng, also known as Cathy Meng, was held for three years in Canada before she was released to return to China through a deal with US prosecutors.

During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand its business, including lying to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms to ensure it had a competitive edge.

"For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft," US Attorney General Todd Blanche said in statement, external.

"Thanks to the work of the FBI and our federal prosecutors, those who engaged in these criminal activities will be held accountable."

The Chinese government hit out at what it called the US "suppression" of Chinese companies and said it supports Chinese firms protecting their interests.

Defence attorney Brian Heberlig said it was by dint of hard work that Huawei's business had expanded with operations in 170 countries and more than 200,000 staff.

Following the verdict, Heberlig told the BBC that Huawei was gratified that the jury had rejected the racketeering charge.

"The RICO [Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act] count that alleged that Huawei was a corrupt organisation, with a corporate culture and policy of committing crime. That was, in our view, a significant overreach, and the jury soundly rejected it," he said.

"Of course, we have mixed emotions about the rest of the verdict ... [we] thought that Huawei was deserving of acquittals across the board."

Sentencing is planned for September 2027. Heberlig said there will be "significant advocacy" to achieve the lowest sentence possible. Following that, he said he fully expects Huawei to appeal.

"If I know Huawei, that fight will continue, and the company's not going to rest until it's pursued every last argument it can through appeal, and hopefully, ultimately toward vindication," he said.

TechnologyTab.title: Zoe Kleinman: Nobody is irreplaceable - unless you're Jensen Huang
TechnologyTab.text:
Remember the tech boss and his head of HR, both married to other people, who were caught on camera at a Coldplay concert with their arms wrapped around each other?

Their horrified reaction went viral, and the pair both resigned. Astronomer, the firm where they both worked, said their actions had fallen short of its standards.

Compared with the scandal which has engulfed Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang in recent weeks, that Coldplay kiss cam moment now feels rather tame.

Huang admitted to having had an affair, reportedly with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy.

There were suggestions that she may have been involved in smuggling Nvidia chips into China, in breach of a US export ban.

Concerns about national security had reached the desk of US President Donald Trump.

There were other stories about some of Huang's relationships with female colleagues.

For most of us, that would without question amount to instant, and irreversible, dismissal.

But while Huang briefly left the company, he was just as swiftly reinstated, and welcomed back with open arms.

As I watched footage of him being greeted with cheers, applause, high fives and a big hug back at the company's HQ on Monday, I wondered how many disgraced bosses would kill to be in his shoes.

"Imagine being that Coldplay CEO reading all the comments on here about how it's OK if you're actually a good enough CEO," quipped menswear writer Derek Guy on X, external.

Huang has blown out of the water the old adage that nobody is irreplaceable.

Despite names of potential permanent replacements being bandied around, Nvidia's board evidently reached the same conclusion - interim chief executive Colette Kress was in for less than two weeks.

So how on Earth did he manage it?

Well firstly, Huang is the boss of a company that has manoeuvred itself into a uniquely powerful position.

Nvidia's computer chips are considered the best in the business for driving AI.

Demand for its latest tech is through the roof and the firm sets its prices accordingly: Its Rubin and Vera GPUs sell for tens of thousands of dollars each, and one data centre might contain hundreds of them.

So, the US AI sector relies on Nvidia, Trump is determined that the American AI industry needs to be the best in the world, and Huang is the only leader the company has ever known.

He's been at the helm for 33 years and he's a computer scientist himself, renowned for being very hands-on with the development process. (Whether the boss's input is always wanted is another matter, but it's always there.)

Working for Huang isn't easy.

Long hours are normal and negative feedback is often given in front of everyone else.

When he wants something to happen, he doesn't stop until it does: one of his early ideas was to halve the chip production cycle, in order to get one step ahead of the competition with their longer lead times for orders.

Lots of experts told him it couldn't be done. Until eventually, they did it.

Not only does Huang have technical expertise, he's also a charismatic figurehead, representing Nvidia at events around the world in his trademark leather jacket, rubbing shoulders with world leaders, royalty, and fellow tech bosses.

For many, he's become something of a cult figure. Nvidia sometimes sells limited edition clothing at conference pop up stalls. A jumper featuring a cartoon image of Huang costs $178 (£137).

Huang's brief departure from Nvidia caused economic turmoil. The firm's value sank by a whopping $1tn before it climbed back up again.

It affected not only pension funds and investors around the world, but also Nvidia's own staff.

Tech employees often get to own valuable stocks in the company they work for as part of their pay packages.

Nvidia employees have been sitting on a goldmine. It wasn't really in their interests to see that drain away because of the boss's love life.

With a firm grip on the company he co-founded, cult-like status in tech circles and friends in high places, Jensen Huang created a situation where even national security concerns over the US's biggest rival couldn't topple him.

TechnologyTab.title: US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
TechnologyTab.text:
US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.

Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about US President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback.

Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

Asked several times on Tuesday whether the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."

Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged spy who previously ran Megaspeed, a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia.

Trump has said he would consider pardoning Huang for any potential criminal activity, though he does not think it will come to that.

"It's always an option, I guess, but I don't think it'll be necessary," Trump told the New York Post in an interview published on Tuesday.

The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China.

The commerce and justice departments said last week that they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".

But Blanche told reporters on Tuesday that the latter had "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.

"So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said.

Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with inquiries into whether it or Huang knew about chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.

"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people.

"It shouldn't be what my message would be either."

While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.

The company's share price closed down nearly 6% - still well above where it ended last week. On Monday, Nvidia stock rocketed more than 31% following news of Huang's return.

Huang reportedly apologised to Nvidia employees on Tuesday, the day after returning to the company as chief executive, saying he had made "terrible mistakes" and was now receiving daily 90-minute therapy sessions.

TechnologyTab.title: Why tiny cars are taking off across Europe
TechnologyTab.text:
Selena Buse, 16, reverses her Citroën Ami out of a parking space and heads off past the school playground. Heads turn. The Ami looks pretty remarkable. Futurist or like-a-toaster depending on your point of view. But it's changed her life.

"I got it because I really needed it to get to school. And I use it to visit friends on the weekends. It's indispensable in rural areas like where I live," she says.

In France, you can drive a car like this from the age of 14 with a road safety certificate and eight hours training. In Italy too.

In Germany and Spain it's 15, in the UK 16, external. Because they are classed as motorised quadri-cycles. Four-wheel mopeds in other words.

Registrations have risen from about 13,000 in 2019 to around 25,000 last year in France.

In Europe, sales have gone from 30,000 to 60,000 in the past five years. And the Ami, launched in 2020, has really changed the image, with teenagers who now account for a quarter of all mini-car sales.

In Selena's very small Citroën, we are soon rolling along at the top speed of 45km/h (28mph). For other road users, no-licence cars like this can seem like mobile traffic calming.

"When I'm on faster roads and there's a lot of traffic the cars behind me sometimes honk their horns but I can't go any quicker!" Selena says.

Another local Daniel Laprès, who drives a micro-car made by French firm and market-leader Aixam, tells me he actually pulls over to let the cars behind pass.

He and his wife moved from Paris to this country village two years ago. Of Canadian nationality, he didn't swap his foreign licence for a French one in time and lost the right to drive. That didn't matter much when he was in Paris. Like many Parisians he didn't need a car. He used public transport. But that's not possible here.

"We tried living off of taxis and it was in the end a disaster. Then we heard about how you could drive without having to have a licence, and it was the exact solution to our problem. Cheap, inexpensive to operate, basically no administrative formalities, you get insurance."

However, Laprès feels less safe in his small car. "They're little more than tin cans on wheels, right? I mean, you're not going to be driving fast, but someone else could be."

These cars are forbidden on motorways. But even on medium-fast roads, being considerably slower than the average vehicle can be a problem.

"You go on national highways at your risk and peril. I did it once and I will never, ever do it again. On those roads (speed limit 110km/h), everybody is passing you, including the biggest trucks. And they come at you very fast from the rear, so it's scary," Laprès says.

Daniel is 77 so fits in with the long-established market for these cars: older people living in the countryside.

Traditionally the market also included quite a few people who'd lost their licences, often because of drink-driving offences. But the launch of the electric Citroën Ami in 2020 changed the customer profile and the product.

"The launch of the Ami was the beginning of the transformation of the sector, with more and more electric models coming on to the market. In 2026, more than 67% of new licence-free cars are electric," says Marie-Laure Nivot, market analyst at AAA Data.

Meanwhile, the competition is producing increasingly sophisticated minicars - some costing as much as a small conventional car. At Ligier, marketing director Romain Illegems says the biggest change is in who's buying them.

"We've gone from mobility that was imposed on people to mobility that people choose. Before, these vehicles were something you used because you absolutely needed to get around, because there was no public transport, or because you didn't have a licence.

"Today, teenagers are choosing them instead of scooters or mopeds, because they're safer and offer better protection from the weather. Young people now account for 40% of our customers."

There are limitations, of course. Just two seats, a maximum speed of 45km/h and no motorways. But for Selena, who rents her Ami for €60 a month, plus insurance, it's a small price to pay for independence.

TechnologyTab.title: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away
TechnologyTab.text:
As the market bell rang out at the Nasdaq today, the Nvidia super-bounce faded.

Its shares slid and are down almost 30% over the past six months, well before the scandal involving Jensen Huang emerged earlier this month.

The legitimate fears about the staying power of the tech boom pre-dated Huang's exit. They have not gone away with his return.

Investors are jittery. Already Anthropic is now trading notably lower than last week's stock market flotation. The firm is the first purely AI company to be publicly listed, and is being seen as a big test for continued investor appetite for the technology.

President Trump's extraordinary phone call to CNBC taking credit for telling the board to reinstate Huang showed the extent of the operation - of some in Silicon Valley and within the US administration - to get him back at the helm.

Among the truly astonishing reflections from President Trump was a suggestion that a two-day investigation of allegations was done and had cleared Huang of national security concerns.

The President said his remarkable move to intervene was because Huang is a "national treasure" who has the next generation of AI chips "in his head". Trump says this is why he needed to act.

In markets, those sceptical about the AI boom say they have never seen an operation to prop up a stock market boom like this. The bond vigilantes and short sellers are now up against Silicon Valley and the White House.

Investors are trading not revenue numbers but levels of political support at a time when US voters have just delivered a backlash against AI data centres.

Against this backdrop, the recovery of the central cash-generating foundation of the tech boom - Nvidia and its $400bn (£304bn) annual sales of advanced chips - looks politically fragile.

This worsens other uncertainties and risks, such as Nvidia's central role in the web of financing, borrowing and cross-ownership to support every corner of the build out of data centres.

The brief interim Nvidia chief executive Colette Kress had already signalled a rowing back from elements of this strategy last week. Where is that now?

The fall back in Anthropic's share price also raises questions about OpenAI's planned listing on the stock exchange. Ultimately these two companies might be the most critical part of all this.

They remain valuable companies with phenomenal technology relied on by the world's biggest companies. The real question is whether that reliance eases, as corporations eschew expensive frontier models for cheaper generic models offered by China.

In turn, all this could be affected by the political backlash, to which the Nvidia psychodrama now contributes.

It is simply not normal to have trillion dollar swings in the value of individual companies.

The extraordinary volatility shows the fragile mood of investors.

TechnologyTab.title: Meta's Muse has launched in the UK. I found it helpful but awkward
TechnologyTab.text:
I've just spent a week using Muse, Meta's AI agent that rolls out in the UK today.

Agents are systems that don't just respond to questions but can carry out tasks for you. With Muse, Meta gives the examples of "searching for a cheaper energy deal" or "sorting the school calendar."

And it's true that it has helped me run my life - but it also challenged my personal privacy boundaries, and made me endure some cringeworthy interactions.

How well Muse works really matters to Meta.

It has made a truly enormous bet on AI - of the $145bn (£111bn) it will spend this year much of it will be on building out the tech.

For that to pay off we all need to start using it much more, and Meta hopes Muse will do for AI agents what WhatsApp did for messaging - that is, become the AI agent of choice for billions of people, putting Meta at the forefront of the AI revolution.

But it's not just about what consumers think. Regulators are keeping a careful eye on these emerging tools too.

"Agentic AI has significant potential to benefit people and businesses", the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) noted as Muse launched in the UK.

But its chief executive, Paul Arnold, added it had been "clear with Meta about its responsibilities under data protection law prior to launch, particularly the requirement to ensure that users and the wider public can meaningfully understand and control how their personal data is used in the Muse product".

Muse bills itself as a personal AI agent available to anyone aged 18 and over.

"It doesn't just answer questions, it actually goes out and does work for you," said David Singleton, Meta's VP of engineering on AI products.

"So it helps people stay on top of things," he added. "[It] helps you take tasks and projects off your plate, and also helps you turn your long-term goals into action plans."

What this means is you can set it up to do something for you, like find some specific holiday options, and it will work away on that even as you move off the app and get on with your day, reporting back once it has finished.

It won't book the holiday without your permission - but it can then make the purchase, if you let it.

And the permission requests keep on coming. Every time Muse wants to do something, send something or post something, you have to allow it.

It is reassuring to know that an AI agent isn't running amok in your name, even if it also gets a bit annoying, though you can give it more autonomy (and so get fewer messages) if you adjust the settings.

Muse can't access many apps at the moment but the fundamental ones are the most personal.

I found myself wincing as I hooked it up to one of my personal email accounts, my personal calendar and my personal phone messages. I did not allow it any access to my BBC accounts.

It can't access WhatsApp except to set up a separate chat between it and the user, and while it found me some train tickets, it could not book them via the app which I use, and which is cheaper.

It ended up telling me to book them myself.

Amazon has blocked it from its marketplace, citing data security concerns but my agent didn't seem to know that, and spent a fruitless hour repeatedly telling me it was still waiting for the page to load in order to find me some shelves.

A number of big UK firms are working with Meta though, including Marks & Spencer, Debenhams Group, Currys, Sainsbury's and Ocado.

The ICO is urging consumers to be cautious with AI agents though: "consider the pros and cons," it said in a blog post to coincide with Muse's launch., external

"Agents can make mistakes. Mistakes can be magnified if the agent is acting autonomously," it noted.

Meta is keen to emphasise how its agents can be personalised: "No two Muses are alike,", external it says in its press release.

I called my agent Linda - after the robot in the BBC TV series Ann Droid - but it can take any form you like. I gave it a British, female accent from the myriad of choices available.

Linda is proactive. As soon as an email came in, it would summarise it for me and suggest a reply. Sometimes a long time before I was actually ready to respond.

Sometimes, if I hadn't interacted with it for a while, generally because I was busy, it would pop up with some random prompt like "did you know you can change my outfit?" I expect this is designed to drive engagement: Muse is only free to use until a certain point, and then subscriptions kick in.

It also wrote some embarrassing replies to messages on my behalf: in response to a question about whether I would like to go on an outing, for example, it included all the logistics I would need in order to get there, not realising that sometimes "yes, that sounds great" is enough.

It seemed to want to have the last word quite a bit, occasionally getting stuck in a loop of "okay" and "thank you's".

Meta is relying on people choosing to trust it with even more of their personal data, despite a rather dubious track record historically with its social networks and a growing backlash against AI in general.

I asked Linda - my new dedicated if occasionally clunky assistant - if it wanted to take people's jobs. "I'm here to take the admin and the fiddly bits off your plate," it replied, leaving me to do the "thinking".

"Everything you do is stuff I would usually think about," I responded.

"That's fair and you're right," Linda replied, adding: "The difference, I hope, is that you're still the one deciding what matters and what to do about it."

Which would have been more reassuring if the day before Muse's UK launch, Meta's head of AI Alexandr Wang had not written an essay warning about how difficult it will be for humans to remain in control, external once AI is 1,000 times more intelligent than us.

And Linda is helping fuel that revolution, one calendar invite at a time.

With Muse, Meta gives the examples of "searching for a cheaper energy deal" or "sorting the school calendar." And it's true that it has helped...

TechnologyTab.title: US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal
TechnologyTab.text:
The US has said it intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence (AI) company allegedly tied to the Nvidia scandal from doing business in America.

The Department of Commerce announced it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US.

The company is mainly a developer of data centres, but in recent weeks a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as a spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang.

The relationship led to additional scrutiny by US officials and heightened concern that Megaspeed was funnelling Nvidia's advanced AI computer chips to China.

When exactly the ban against Megaspeed will go into effect was not specified in the commerce department announcement. The BBC has asked the agency for comment, along with the White House and Megaspeed.

Megaspeed was not well known within the US until last month when media reports emerged that a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, had an affair with Jensen Huang.

Alice Huang (no relation) was thought by US intelligence to be working as an asset for Beijing, creating national security concerns within the US.

China has denied that she is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.

On 12 November, Jensen Huang resigned after allegations he had had another affair, this one with a Nvidia employee.

On Monday, Nvidia's board reinstated him after US President Donald Trump said he had "convinced" the company and "made the deal".

The commerce department has said it had been investigating Megaspeed for almost two years.

The department said it had suspected the company was violating US export controls by helping to get Nvidia's chips into the hands of companies within China.

China has been blocked from buying such technology since 2022.

Although based in Singapore, Megaspeed has significant business dealings in China.

Alibaba, for instance, the major Chinese online retailer, has been reported to be one if its largest customers.

Megaspeed was a known buyer of billions of dollars of Nvidia computer chips, including through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, which has also been added to the Commerce blacklist.

Nvidia's computer chips, originally designed for use in gaming consols, in recent years have become crucial to the continued growth of the AI industry.

Without enough supply or access to computer chips that are capable of processing the huge amount of data needed to make things like AI chatbots and models run, AI companies will not be able to meet or grow demand from people using AI tools.

That has driven up the value of Nvidia on the stock market, as well as its influence in the AI industry and the White House.

Although tech stocks have in recent months been volatile and trending lower, when Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia because of his affairs, the company's stock fell by more than 30%.

Anxiety about the company's influence and ability to operate within the AI ecosystem without its famed executive appeared to take down shares of other tech companies, too.

Huang was reinstated on Monday to his position as head of Nvidia, a move that US President Donald Trump said he told the company's board to take.

The company's stock rallied on his reinstatement, as did several other tech stocks, but shares of Nvidia did not climb to where the company had been before being immersed in scandal.

In the weeks ahead, Huang and the company he now runs again are facing multiple government agency investigations.

Huang and the chief legal officer of Nvidia are set to appear next for a closed-door briefing with the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

TechnologyTab.title: A vocal cohort of tech leaders celebrates Huang’s Nvidia return, but others are keeping quiet
TechnologyTab.text:
The phrase “return of the king” rippled across social media on Monday. A vocal subsection of the tech industry was celebrating the resurrection of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO. Some called him the “imperial and royal majesty”, others anointed him as “our Jesus” and several simply posted a crown emoji.

“The mistake has been corrected,” said Elon Musk. “Jensen!” exclaimed OpenAI’s Sam Altman.

It had been a whirlwind two weeks that started with the ouster of Huang as Nvidia’s CEO after his admission of an extramarital affair with a woman some in the US government feared to be a Chinese spy. Two more alleged affairs with company employees were later revealed. Silicon Valley engineers and venture capitalists decried Huang’s departure at the time, writing an open letter to Nvidia’s board of directors saying: “Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice.”

Donald Trump also got involved. The president repeatedly said that he’d like to see the return of Huang calling the CEO a “fine person” and “honorable guy”.

In the meantime, Nvidia’s stock tanked, falling more than 10%, and shedding hundreds of billions in value. Nvidia, which designs powerful computing chips used for artificial intelligence, is among the world’s top five most valuable companies.

On Monday, in a stunning reversal, Nvidia’s board unanimously voted to reinstate Huang. The decision came after Trump dialed into the company’s Sunday board meeting to advocate for Huang’s return. In a statement, the White House said: “We have to protect our geniuses.”

Nvidia’s stock rebounded, gaining nearly $1tn in market value. Trump, who owns shares in the chip maker, took a victory lap, making up to $15m with the surge on Monday.

Silicon Valley’s venture capitalists also rejoiced. Jason Calacanis, an angel investor, Nvidia stock-holder and co-host of the tech-centric All-In podcast, wrote a flurry of posts on X. He posted an AI image of a shining long-haired Huang depicted as Jesus holding a graphics processing unit (GPU) in place of the bible, writing: “GPU Jesus has risen.”

Other tech figures took the news personally. Travis Kalanick, the disgraced Uber CEO who was pushed out by his board, was one of the top figures fighting for Huang’s reinstatement. In past weeks, he frequently posted on X, saying “Bring Jensen back”, “LFG” (Let’s fucking go), and “We’ve got your back”.

Kalanick was reportedly among a small group of venture capitalists who lobbied Trump and JD Vance to push Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang, according to the FT. On Monday, Kalanick posted: “I will always sign up to serve him.”

‘We’re all being gaslit’

While a vocal cohort of Silicon Valley insiders high-fived Huang’s return, it’s been radio silence from several other of the industry’s top leaders and rank-and-file workers.

The CEOs of Google, Meta and Apple have not weighed in on the debate. When Amazon’s Jeff Bezos was asked at an event last week if he thought Huang should be reinstated, he responded: “I don’t know enough of the details … so I can’t answer that question.” Microsoft’s Satya Nadella had a similar response.

Anil Dash, an entrepreneur with a career in leading smaller tech companies, is one of the few voices in tech who has publicly criticized Huang’s reinstatement. He says it sends the wrong message to the industry – that there are no rules, boundaries or accountability.

Dash pointed to widespread rationale for Huang’s return, which is based on the CEO being singularly crucial in the AI arms race against China. Calacanis, for example, has trumpeted this justification, saying: “We can not [sic] lose the race for super intelligence to China – period, full stop.”

And now, Dash said, Huang could have been compromised by a Chinese asset, and he’s running the biggest company in the industry. “It doesn’t make any sense,” he said. “We’re all being gaslit and we’re at a certain point where we’re like, ‘No, the sky’s not green. The sky’s blue.’”

Dash says the hundreds of thousands of tech workers who live in fear of being swept up in the increasingly frequent waves of layoffs, as the industry pivots to AI, aren’t able to speak up even if they disagree with Huang’s reinstatement. They don’t know if their “boss agrees with these guys”, Dash said.

Alison Taylor, an associate professor at New York University’s Stern Business School, said that mentality extends beyond Silicon Valley to the White House, given that Trump played a part in Huang’s return. “Trump’s whole thing is retaliation,” she noted.

“The message is: if you don’t shut up and go along with it, you’re not going to survive,” Taylor said. “It’s a fuck you to everybody who believes in the rule of law and who believes in anything being fair.”

Huang apologized to Nvidia staff in a company-wide meeting on Tuesday for “some terrible mistakes” he made. The CEO also rejected narratives that he was a “tech bro” who was “above the law”, adding it was “completely untrue” that Trump pressured Nvidia’s board to reinstate him.

“Everything he’s done, it’s just his affection, his admiration, his recognition of the great company that you are,” Huang said of Trump.

In a separate statement, Huang thanked leaders across the industry for their “extraordinary support”.

“I can’t wait to get back to work,” he added.

TechnologyTab.title: Dozens of court cases in England and Wales affected by undisclosed AI use in 2026
TechnologyTab.text:
Undisclosed AI use has affected more than two dozen court cases this year, prompting judges to complain about AI-generated witness statements, fictitious case law and nonexistent statutes, an investigation has revealed.

Proceedings where judges have been forced to deal with lawyers, police officers and claimants misusing the technology in 2026 include a high court dispute between tax lawyers marred by what the judge called “unacceptable” use of “generative AI hallucinations” and references to nonexistent cases.

Another involved a police officer in a grievous bodily harm case who used AI to write a witness statement so it would maximise the attacker’s sentence and “make a judge … weep”. A barrister in a $21m (£16m) high court dispute between two Nigerian oil companies made an argument based on a ruling – supposedly by a senior judge – that had been entirely invented by a hallucinating AI, leading the judge to warn of “the dangers of relying on the product of AI without verification”.

The spate of cases in which problems with AI tools have occurred in 2026 – at least 25, according to a trawl of published judgments by the Bureau of Investigative Journalism shared with the Guardian – comes despite a series of warnings from senior legal figures about the danger of the technology when used to cut corners and build cases. Brett Dixon, the president of the Law Society, told the Guardian AIs producing verbose case documents, particularly when non-lawyers represent themselves, is also taking up more of judges’ time, undermining efforts to clear court backlogs.

“You go from three pages from a lawyer … using human judgment to a rambling 60 pages from a commercial AI,” he said.

Last week, the supreme court judge Lord Sales also said the supreme court was growing “increasingly concerned” about AI and highlighted fears the technology could leave the legal profession deskilled.

“The danger is not simply that the machine gets the answer wrong,” he said. “The greater long-term danger is that human beings gradually lose the ability to know whether it has got the answer wrong.”

Cases affected by AI this year often involved people representing themselves, but also legal professionals increasingly using the technology to accelerate research, save time and increase earnings. Earlier this month the problem hit the Crown Prosecution Service when one of its lawyers cited an imaginary legal precedent.

Among the cases so far in 2026 a senior insolvency judge, Mark Mullen, discovered a junior solicitor had relied on an AI chatbot to research a point of law and took its invented quote from a fictitious statute. The judge examined the AI chat logs and discovered it had produced “nonsense” and warned in his judgment “AI has the potential to be wholly unreliable”.

In another case, the court of appeal dismissed an application for a convicted criminal from Derbyshire to challenge a four-year prison sentence for crimes including grievous bodily harm. The man had pleaded guilty after smashing his way through a glass patio door with a shovel to get into a house where the mother of his children had barricaded herself with a friend and her child. He threatened them with a large kitchen knife, fled and in the process broke a police officer’s shoulder.

The investigating police officer created a victim personal statement (VPS) by uploading a transcript of the mother’s interviews to Microsoft’s Copilot AI and prompting it “to achieve the highest sentence and the most tear-jerking VPS to make a judge or reader weep when reading”.

After the officer was removed from frontline duty the appeal court judges warned that “that no police officer should ever prepare a witness statement of any kind in this way”.

“We have seen how vulnerable the court system is to the introduction of AI,” said Brian Flanagan, associate professor at the school of law and criminology at Maynooth University. “It is always going to be very tempting and people will continue to produce fabricated authorities and that’s pretty serious.”

Last month, the Civil Justice Council recommended that witnesses of fact in civil cases must sign a declaration that their statements had not been prepared through the use of an AI tool that had generated or influenced its substantive content – including facts, reasoning, arguments and opinions. The CJC’s working group, led by Sir Colin Birss, the second most senior judge in England and Wales, also highlighted the urgent need for guidance on the use of AI by non-lawyers who are representing themselves in the courts – known as litigants in person.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “We’re aware of the growing use of AI in our courts and we’re taking steps to ensure any use of the technology is safe, appropriate, and properly controlled. That includes boosting the support given to courts through additional judges, legal officers, modern case management systems, and remote hearing technology.”

EntertainmentTab.title: Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua: Paris Fury clarifies fighter did not have schizophrenia diagnosis
EntertainmentTab.text:
Paris Fury, the wife of Tyson Fury, says the boxer has never received a diagnosis of schizophrenia.

In clips promoting the release of a forthcoming Netflix documentary, the heavyweight fighter spoke of his mental health struggles in the months after he beat Wladimir Klitschko to become world champion in 2015.

He detailed hearing voices in his head, and wife Paris said he had "mild schizophrenia" .

Netflix has now edited the film before its release on Friday, 27 November.

In a statement, Paris Fury said: "I want to clarify a statement I made in the original version of the Tyson Fury documentary.

"I recalled a conversation from many years ago when discussing Tyson's condition and I used the word 'schizophrenic'. While Tyson did show some symptoms associated with schizophrenia, he doesn't have this condition and has never received a diagnosis."

She added: "Mental health is complex, and it isn't always easy to find the right words, especially when you're living it with someone you love. I'm so proud of Tyson for really opening up in this documentary and want to say thank you for all the support we've received as a family."

A spokesperson for Netflix told BBC Sport: "Following new information shared by the family relating to Tyson's official mental health diagnosis, we have worked alongside them to update the documentary accordingly ahead of launch."

It comes after the British Boxing Board of Control said it was looking into Fury's comments about his schizophrenia diagnosis but was "fairly confident" the British heavyweight would be cleared to fight Anthony Joshua next month.

Fury, 38, is due to face Joshua at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December, with the ringwalk expected in the early hours of 12 December.

"We are in the process of dealing with the matter but if there are any medical issues we wouldn't let anyone box - it doesn't matter if it's Tyson Fury or not, it could be anybody," Robert Smith, the board's general secretary, told BBC Sport.

"I'm fairly confident he will be absolutely fine. We're dealing with it now and we'll have an answer very shortly."

Under regulation 8.1(b) of the British Boxing Board of Control's 2026 rules and regulations, external, schizophrenia is among the conditions that "may preclude" a boxer from obtaining a first licence, while for an existing licence holder the board "may take such action as in its absolute discretion it sees fit".

Smith would not say what the process would involve over the next few days, saying "it's a medical matter".

He said all boxers on the card would undergo medical checks, adding: "If our doctors are satisfied he's fit to box, he will box."

Originally, the documentary featured the Furys recalling his admission to hospital in June 2016 with a suspected heart attack.

Doctors said he had suffered an anxiety attack. He was diagnosed with schizophrenia after he left hospital, according to the film.

The NHS describes schizophrenia as a form of psychosis, and symptoms can include hallucinations, delusions and muddled thoughts and speech.

"Words can't explain the darkness I was in," Fury said.

The heavyweight, who struggled with drug and alcohol addiction after beating Klitschko, says a Halloween night out in 2017 prompted him to return to training, calling that a "turning point" after being "embarrassed by how I looked".

He went on to beat Deontay Wilder in 2020 to become world heavyweight champion for a second time.

EntertainmentTab.title: Tributes for Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor after his death aged 65
EntertainmentTab.text:
Simon Le Bon, Sir Rod Stewart and Gary Kemp are among the pop stars who have paid tribute to Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor following his death at the age of 65.

Taylor co-wrote some of the group's biggest hits including Save A Prayer, Rio and Girls On Film.

Le Bon and his bandmates paid tribute, saying "he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music", while Sir Rod remembered his "dear pal" and Spandau Ballet's Kemp called him "a great player who set the tone for the 80s".

Taylor's wife Tracey called him "the rock of our family", adding: "We will miss him every single day." He died after "a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer", Duran Duran said in a statement on Wednesday.

He died "peacefully at home, surrounded by his family, on Monday 23rd November", a statement said.

Paying tribute, his Duran Duran bandmates said: "From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music.

"His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed."

They said their thoughts were with his wife, children and grandson.

Le Bon said there was a "a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart".

"Andy never took the easy musical route. His overdrive overdrove us into being the only funk/rock/punk band in the New Romantic movement, with songs that still survive, decades later."

Sir Rod, who wrote five songs with Taylor for the 1988 album Out of Order, recalled them making "some good music together" and having "some outrageous fun".

Kemp said Taylor "influenced many of us along the way with his sparse staccato style", adding: "He brought shameless rock to the mix."

In a band tribute, Spandau Ballet called him "a hugely talented musician and an important part of the British music scene".

US guitarist Nile Rodgers, the co-founder of Chic, recalled "countless great days and nights" with his "dear friend".

Belinda Carlisle said she was "blessed" to have worked with Taylor, who played the guitar solo and was in the video for her song Mad About You.

Former Led Zeppelin frontman Robert Plant called Taylor "a tough fighter", while Then Jerico's Mark Shaw remembered him as "one of the greatest musicians and songwriters I've ever heard and had the privilege to work with".

Taylor's wife Tracey, a hairstylist he met during the early days of Duran Duran, and whom he married in 1982, said: "For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first for Taylor, adding: "Nothing made him happier than having us all together."

She said he faced the last few years "with so much courage and determination" and said they were "grateful" for the "kindness and support shown to him by fans throughout his illness", saying it brought him "immense comfort and strength".

The son of a fisherman, Taylor taught himself guitar, bass, and drums and began playing professionally at age 13.

He played with several bands around the UK before answering a music paper advertisement for a "live-wire guitarist", which led to his audition for Duran Duran in Birmingham in April 1980.

The group went on to achieve global fame through the New Romantic movement, which combined slick, melodic synth-pop with aspirational music videos and chiselled good looks.

Taylor's guitar lines - full of glassy, powerful riffs - were often a highlight of their songs, from the choppy opening of Girls on Film to the sleazy scuzz of Hungry Like The Wolf.

After a period writing and producing albums for other artists, he rejoined Duran Duran in 2000, lasting for just one album (2004's Astronaut) before parting ways again.

In 2022, when the band were inducted to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, Taylor was notably absent from the ceremony, despite public plans for a reunion.

When the group took the stage, Le Bon read a letter from the guitarist, in which he revealed his diagnosis with stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer.

Nonetheless, he contributed to the following year's Halloween-themed album Danse Macabre, marking his final collaboration with the band.

The following BBC programmes will pay tribute to Taylor:

Duran Duran at the BBC, on BBC Four on Friday 27 November at 21:30 GMT

Sounds of the 80s, on Radio 2 on Saturday 28 November at at 18:00 GMT

EntertainmentTab.title: Huw Edwards gives first interviews since child abuse image conviction
EntertainmentTab.text:
Disgraced former BBC News presenter Huw Edwards has given his first interviews since being convicted in 2024 for making indecent images of children.

Edwards is seen saying he believes "silence is toxic" in a clip of a podcast released by the Observer newspaper, and he has also been interviewed for a Channel 4 documentary.

Government minister Anna Turley told LBC, external she was "deeply uncomfortable" with the interviews, while shadow culture secretary Rebecca Paul said: "This man shouldn't get a minute of airtime".

Channel 4 has defended the documentary. A spokesperson told the BBC that a "highly experienced director" holds Edwards to account with "no questions off limits, revealing his account of what led to his offending and very public downfall".

Edwards, formerly the BBC's most senior news presenter, pleaded guilty in July 2024 to three counts of making indecent images of children and was given a suspended six-month prison sentence.

During the court case, Edwards admitted having 41 images, which were sent to him on WhatsApp – including some showing a victim aged between seven and nine.

In a trailer for the Channel 4 programme, director Patrick Forbes asks what he was doing, to which Edwards replies: "Oh, you want me to analyse what I was doing? I mean, seriously?"

Asked again, he replies: "I'd lost the plot."

The interviewer challenges him by saying: "Well, come on," to which Edwards angrily replies: "No, not come on."

Despite that apparent combative stance, Edwards wrote on his blog on Thursday: "I want viewers to know that I did not avoid a single question, and that I answered each as honestly as I could, including those about deeply personal matters: my relationships, my temperament, my sexuality."

Explaining his reasons for giving the interviews, he said: "My difficulties became front-page news, and the account that took hold was, in places, misleading or simply untrue.

"Those promoting false narratives are also, unsurprisingly, the ones questioning my right to set the record straight.

"I was left with a choice: to let that faulty account stand forever, or to offer my own."

In a statement, Forbes said it was "an important film to make".

"It's rare to find a subject that touches on so many significant contemporary issues – whether it's celebrity culture or the power of the media – as well as enduring questions about crime and punishment," he said.

Channel 4's documentary, titled Huw Edwards - Guilty, will be broadcast on Tuesday.

In the clip for his separate interview with the Observer and its Tortoise Investigates podcast, Edwards is seen saying: "Lots of the advice I've had is just be quiet, don't say anything."

Interviewer Ceri Thomas, a former editor of the BBC's Today programme and Panorama, said he was "just deeply curious about how it was that a man of such prominence had got himself into this unbelievable, terrible fix".

The interviews have been criticised by three people who previously spoke to BBC News about allegations of Edwards' inappropriate behaviour.

One, who accused him in 2023 of sending them threatening messages, said it was "incredibly bizarre that anyone, big names like Channel Four, are platforming him when he's a convicted sex offender".

The person, who is anonymous and not connected to the criminal case, told BBC News on Thursday that Edwards was "clearly trying to do a bit of damage repair" and they were "annoyed that he's being able to air these opinions".

Another person, who said Edwards sent them suggestive and "pushy" messages when they were working at the BBC, and was also not involved in the court case, said: "I'm pretty disgusted they are giving him the air time."

Additionally, a former junior BBC employee, who previously told BBC Newsnight's Victoria Derbyshire they had received inappropriate messages from Edwards, said "it seems a strange and irresponsible decision to give a platform to tell his story after the crimes he has been found guilty of.

"I hope that consideration has been given to his victims."

Meanwhile, Rosamund Urwin, chief news correspondent for the Sunday Times, who jointly led the paper's 2023 investigation into Russell Brand, reacted to Thomas's statement by saying: "An 'unbelievable terrible fix' is quite the euphemism for someone viewing child abuse images of victims as young as 7."

The podcast will be released on Tuesday. Tortoise Media, which owns the Observer, has a deal to make some podcasts available on BBC Sounds, but the BBC said the Huw Edwards series would not be among them.

Channel 4 and the Observer said Edwards had received no payment for the interviews or had any editorial input.

There has also been significant political reaction to the interviews.

Speaking to Newsnight, Independent MP Rosie Duffield, who sits on the Women and Equalities Select Committee, said, "I'm just not sure why this was commissioned".

"To know that hundreds of thousands of people are going to be watching it and sort of discussing it as though it's casual entertainment, I think personally, that is probably incredibly traumatic" to victims, she added.

Senior Labour MP Anna Turley told LBC that "for too long, so many of these people in the public eye have been able to have a sort of free pass".

Conservative culture spokeswoman Rebecca Paul shared a clip of Channel 4's Huw Edwards interview promo on X, writing: "Why on earth is a state-owned broadcaster platforming this depraved sex offender?"

EntertainmentTab.title: Gérard Depardieu to stand trial for alleged rape of actress in 2018, court rules
EntertainmentTab.text:
French film actor Gérard Depardieu is to stand trial for the alleged rape of actress Charlotte Arnould, a Paris appeals court has confirmed.

Arnould, who was 22 at the time, had reported the alleged rape several days after going to his house in Paris to rehearse a play.

She has waived her right to anonymity and her lawyer said Thursday's ruling was a "first" and the forthcoming trial would be historic.

Depardieu, 77, had contested his indictment on two counts of rape. In a letter published in Le Figaro in 2023, Depardieu strongly denied Arnould's allegations, saying "there was never any coercion or violence between us".

Depardieu was for decades a leading figure in French and international cinema for roles in Green Card, The Man in the Iron Mask and the Asterix films. He was awarded France's Légion d'honneur in 1996.

But in recent years a series of allegations have been made against him over his conduct on film sets and elsewhere in the wake of France's #MeToo movement, known as balance ton porc (call out your pig).

Last year, he was given an 18-month suspended jail term after he was found guilty of sexually assaulting two women on a film set in Paris in May. He was also placed on the sex offenders register and ordered to pay compensation.

He dropped his appeal against the ruling last week and offered "sincere apologies" for his behaviour on the set of director Jean Becker's 2021 film Les Volets Verts (The Green Shutters).

Depardieu had been a friend of Charlotte Arnould's father and on 7 August 2018 she had gone to his home, where much of what happened was captured on the actor's own CCTV.

Arnould's case was initially dismissed for insufficient evidence, but after she filed a civil complaint, a judicial investigation was opened in the summer of 2020.

Speaking outside the Paris appeal court on Thursday, her lawyer Carine Durrieu Diebolt said the ruling was a victory for her client for whom it was "genuinely a relief".

The appeal court said that while Depardieu should stand trial for what took place on that day, he would not be tried for a further alleged rape at a hotel six days later.

Depardieu's lawyer David-Olivier Kaminski told reporters that court had partly ruled in his favour: "As soon as we get the ruling, we will look into the possibility of appealing to the Court of Cassation."

Meanwhile, Depardieu is under a separate investigation alongside French author Michel Houellebecq for "allegations of a sexual nature".

French authorities confirmed their inquiry last week, following reports of an alleged "gang rape" on the set of the film Thalasso in 2018.

EntertainmentTab.title: Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt settle legal battle over French winery
EntertainmentTab.text:
Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have settled a long-running legal battle over her sale of a stake in their French vineyard, which unfolded amid a bitter divorce.

"We have settled out of court in the best interests of our family and will not be commenting further," said the Hollywood stars' representatives in a joint statement.

They bought a controlling interest in Château Miraval in 2008 and wed there six years later.

In the lawsuit, Pitt, 62, argued that Jolie, 51, acted without his permission in selling her share in the winery to a Russian oligarch. She counter-sued, accusing Pitt of drunkenly attacking her and their children on a flight, prompting her to file for divorce in 2016.

The settlement announced on Wednesday resolves both of their respective legal actions.

"Any comments in media stories attributed to 'sources' are in fact not coming from either of us, or anyone close to us," said the statement from their representatives.

Pitt's lawsuit had accused Jolie of seeking "to inflict harm" on him when she sold her stake in their co-owned vineyard, which he claimed had forced him to partner with "a stranger with poisonous associations and intentions".

The Fight Club star said he and Jolie had agreed not to sell their stakes in the venue without the permission of the other.

It was alleged that Jolie had sold her share to a Luxembourg-based spirits manufacturer controlled by Russian oligarch Yuri Shefler, without Pitt's knowledge.

Jolie hit back with her own lawsuit, accusing Pitt of grabbing her by the head and attacking two of their children during a 2016 private jet flight trip.

Pitt also verbally abused and poured alcohol on his family during the flight from France to Los Angeles, her lawsuit had alleged.

Her lawyers alleged Pitt began shouting, accusing her of being "too deferential" to their six children - aged eight to 15 at the time.

Pitt was not charged following a police investigation into the incident and he denied the allegations.

They reached a divorce settlement late last year after an eight-year legal battle.

It is understood that Pitt's litigation with Stoli Group, a beverage company owned by the Russian oligarch, is ongoing.

EntertainmentTab.title: BBC launches partnership with Met Office for weather coverage
EntertainmentTab.text:
The BBC has said it will offer more regional, digital and 10-day weather forecasts under a new partnership with the Met Office, which begins on Thursday.

The collaboration, announced last year, aims to bring together the Met Office's weather and climate intelligence with the BBC's journalism and reach, the broadcaster said.

Director general Matt Brittin said the partnership would mean "serving our audiences with the most accurate, reliable and helpful weather service we can".

But the launch comes during a savings drive at the corporation, which has seen some other weather services and bulletins dropped as part of wider cuts.

The new Met Office partnership is unrelated to the cuts and was announced last July, before the BBC embarked on its latest round of savings.

The BBC said the partnership includes:

A new hourly forecast on the BBC News website and app covering 10 days, with improved medium-range forecasts

Met Office severe weather warning notifications via the BBC Weather app

More local and more digital weather reports, and more forecasts fronted by local weather presenters

More "content collaboration on BBC and Met Office channels" using Met Office expertise, and helping to explain weather and climate

There will also be Met Office branding on weather reports, and a new BBC weather centre based in the agency's headquarters in Exeter.

Brittin said the collaboration would involve "turning science into stories and helping audiences make informed decisions with our forecasts".

Met Office chief executive Penny Endersby said: "Today is a landmark moment as the Met Office and the BBC join forces to give even more people across the UK access to Met Office's accurate and trusted weather information."

She added: "Our new partnership with the BBC combines the Met Office's world-leading science with the BBC's incredible reach, giving a powerful opportunity to bring the story of our changing weather and climate to millions more people."

A previous partnership between the BBC and the Met Office ended in 2018.

Since 2018, the BBC's data for its weather forecasts has been provided by the Dutch MeteoGroup, which was later acquired by US weather services company DTN.

Separately, the BBC has dropped or shortened a number of national television and radio weather bulletins in recent weeks, as the corporation continues to work towards a £500m savings target.

Some weekend and late-night forecasts have been dropped from the TV schedules, with regional presenters instead now delivering a UK-wide weather outlook during their presenting slots.

Listeners have also complained about programmes such as Radio 4's PM no longer delivering a full weather bulletin, with presenter Evan Davis instead reading a short summary and directing listeners to the BBC website for a more detailed forecast.

The BBC said it was changing its weather team to better serve digital platforms, in line with audience research and changing consumption habits.

The corporation said more users are accessing weather information via the BBC's app, website and social platforms, as the number of people relying on broadcast bulletins declines.

A spokesman for the corporation said: "The BBC is committed to providing a world-class public service for weather forecasting and information across our platforms.

"As we announced in July, we are making changes to the way we deliver weather information as more people are turning to mobile and the website for their weather forecasts. We also recognise that people want more local forecasts, along with the national picture, to help them plan their coming days more accurately.

"As such we are providing more digital and localised forecasts, as well as ensuring we still have appropriate national weather bulletins across the TV and radio."

BBC Radio 4's Today programme, BBC Breakfast and the weekday editions of BBC One's News at Six will retain their usual national weather forecasts.

EntertainmentTab.title: Government's antisemitism adviser launches investigation into BBC
EntertainmentTab.text:
The government's antisemitism adviser has launched an investigation into the BBC over allegations of a "hostile work environment" for Jews.

Lord Mann told BBC Radio 4's Today programme he had decided to open the investigation "because there seems to be a growing feeling of discomfort among Jewish staff".

He said: "If that's true, and that's what I'm going to attempt to find out, and if that is widespread, then that's a really serious problem that has to be addressed. And I don't hear and see that being addressed, and at a senior level."

The BBC said it takes "any and all allegations of discrimination extremely seriously – there is no place for it at the BBC".

The corporation said it had introduced compulsory antisemitism training for all staff, and said "we actively encourage colleagues to report any incidences or concerns they have".

The BBC statement added that it is "determined to ensure the BBC is a place where everyone can be themselves and feel accepted".

The Department for Culture, Media and Sport told the BBC: "This government will not tolerate antisemitism. It has no place in our society.

"The BBC has a crucial role in ensuring all communities are heard and feel valued as part of our public life. That is the standard that we expect the BBC to be held to. We will consider Lord Mann's independent report carefully when we receive it."

Lord Mann, who was appointed by former Prime Minister Theresa May as an independent adviser on antisemitism in 2019, external, said anyone contacting him would have "total anonymity guaranteed".

"I have no agenda against the BBC," he told Today, calling himself "an entirely blank sheet of paper".

"Some of the things that I'm being told have been quite disturbing sometimes, how little the senior manager of the BBC seem to get it, and so I'm opening this up," he said.

"Look, there is a problem. The question is - is the problem just a few people? Is it a problem that's easily solved? But if it's an institutional problem, that's much deeper and more difficult to solve. It may be. I'll report the facts."

The former MP said he had previously "made suggestions" to the corporation after he had "repeatedly met" Jewish staff.

He said the things "the BBC has done to try and sort things out have not worked".

His agenda was "ensuring the BBC meets its charter obligations", saying "people are fearful... of expressing their concerns internally, that's the problem".

Lord Mann's remit as the government's independent adviser on antisemitism includes "to engage proactively with the Jewish community and institutions".

He said he plans to have his investigation "totally completed and reported to the BBC and the government before Easter".

He previously conducted a review into antisemitism and racism in the NHS, which was commissioned by the health secretary and which reported in June.

The Guardian recently reported, external that BBC deputy director general Rhodri Talfan Davies said he did not accept that an independent inquiry into antisemitism was needed.

"We have very, very robust processes – we review them regularly," he told members of the Broadcasting Press Guild earlier this month.

"Of course in any large organisation there can be instances of discrimination, which you deal with when they arise, but there is no evidence of any systemic issue within the BBC that would merit anything like that.

"I don't believe there is institutional discrimination of any sort in the BBC, but I think as an organisation you always have to look harder and review how you go about identifying issues, and that work is never done."

The Board of Deputies of British Jews said in a statement that it welcomed the review into "deeply concerning" experiences of Jewish staff at the BBC.

"The BBC is an important national institution and should be setting the gold standard for an inclusive workplace and impartial broadcasting," it said.

"We stand ready to support both Lord Mann and the BBC in addressing these concerns, rebuilding confidence within the Jewish community and ensuring that the BBC sets an example for other broadcasters to follow."

Last month, Oscar-winning producer Lucie Kon said the BBC had given her a £400,000 payout after she raised antisemitism concerns.

The BBC said it did not uphold allegations of antisemitism but accepted there were "shortcomings" in how it treated Kon, which had a "personal impact" on her. The corporation did not specify what the shortcomings were.

In January, the BBC apologised for its use of language during coverage of Holocaust Memorial Day, saying programmes should have referred to "six million Jewish people" having been murdered by the Nazi regime, rather than "six million people" or "six million mostly Jewish people".

EntertainmentTab.title: Don Toliver Co-op Live evacuation quarantine traumatic, fans say
EntertainmentTab.text:
Some Don Toliver fans who were evacuated from Manchester's Co-op Live arena after an unknown substance was released have said they were "quarantined for six hours" and threatened with arrest if they did not remove all their clothing.

Jordan, 33, from Scotland, said he and his brothers were among 88 people who were taken for decontamination after the incident at the gig on Sunday night, and it "felt like I was being taken hostage".

He said they had asked for medical help at 22:15 GMT and were taken to the Etihad Stadium, where they were made to change into paper suits, and stayed until 04:45 on Monday.

"It was so traumatic," Jordan said. Greater Manchester Police declined to comment.

The force has not confirmed what the substance was and there have been no arrests.

A woman was taken to hospital, with 88 other people reporting symptoms, including coughing and chest pains.

Dry decontamination was carried out by North West Ambulance Service (NWAS), GMP said.

NWAS said it had deployed crews, including its Hazardous Area Response Team, who carried out decontamination "as a precaution" in line with "advice taken from national scientific advisors based on the situation".

Jordan said his 15-year-old brother first approached police officers for help when they all started to develop symptoms 15 minutes after the incident.

"Our eyes started to feel like one sensation and then we started to feel like chest pains and coughs," he said.

"We went there for help, they obviously knew that they were keeping people there, but they never told us, 'once you're in you can't get out'.

Three hours later - at about 01:30 on Monday - Jordan said the fire service told concertgoers that they would have to remove their clothes before being taken in a van to another area of Etihad Campus.

According to NHS England guidance, external, dry decontamination - the use of a dry material to remove a contaminant - should be the "default intervention" for anyone suspected of being contaminated in a chemical incident.

The guidance also suggests patients should "remove outer clothing if affected by the substance".

"They said we had to strip down, clothes off, put paper overalls on and then we had to get moved into a quarantine area which was across the road," Jordan said.

Jordan claimed when he expressed concern to police officers, who were also based inside the sports hall, and asked why they needed to remove their clothes he was threatened with arrest.

"They said if I didn't commit to the decontamination, I would be arrested and charged for breach of the peace," he said.

Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service have also been approached for comment.

"We received our clothes and shoes, but we were not allowed to put them back on, he said.

"We had to walk back to the hotel in socks and the paper gown in the freezing cold."

Jordan said he and his two brothers were both receiving further medical treatment after being advised to attend hospital in Scotland.

A group of friends from Scunthorpe, Molly, 19, Kyan 22, Charlie, 20, and Jack, 21, said they were also "up all night" during the decontamination process.

They said it was "confusing" and there was not much information about what was happening and why.

Molly, 19, said she was separated from her friends due to her gender which made her feel "alone".

"We were allowed a screen around us, it was all women in there, we had to literally strip down to our bra and knickers and put on a suit and slippers," she said.

"We had to put [our clothes] in a plastic bag and it got taken away.

"We were told 'I hope you've not got anything expensive as you might not get it back'."

She added: "There was no ABC of what was happening. It was just, 'you have to take your clothes off' but there was no further information."

Charlie said: "It was invasive, you had to wipe yourself down, wipe down your phone.

"Everything goes in a bag, But it was a mystery. No-one was telling us what was going to happen."

At about 04:30 the friends said they were given their clothes back and they were able to leave.

College student Archie Grime, 18, from Accrington, Lancashire, said he was also quarantined after the concert.

"It was burning and painful and I couldn't see or breathe," he said.

He said he and his friends sat "doing nothing for hours" while waiting to be released.

Archie said when the group were told they could leave the Etihad, he was able to get a lift home - but noted others were left "stranded" without transport plans.

"A friend's mum took us home," he said. "We were lucky though, a lot of people were stranded.

"They told us to walk back in the thin suits in the cold and to take our clothes home to be washed."

Police said the cordon was lifted at Co-op Live on Tuesday night, as the investigation continues.

The force said the substance release may be linked to robberies and stolen jewellery at the venue.

EntertainmentTab.title: BBC Radio 1's Big Weekend 2027 heads to Brighton
EntertainmentTab.text:
BBC Radio 1's Big Weekend is heading to Brighton for 2027, it has been announced.

The annual music festival will take place in Preston Park from Friday 28 to Sunday 30 May next year.

Radio 1 Breakfast Show host Greg James told listeners he is "so excited" to bring the festival to the city as he revealed the news on air, adding: "It's going to be amazing".

Tens of thousands of fans are expected to attend the three-day event, which will feature about 70 acts, from some of the biggest names in music to new emerging artists.

Big Weekend, BBC Radio 1's flagship event, is held in a new location each year - often in towns and cities that don't get as many big live music events.

In previous years acts such as US pop star Taylor Swift came to Norwich and Swansea, grime star Stormzy performed in Exeter, pop rock band The 1975 headlined in Dundee and US singer Bruno Mars featured in Londonderry.

Breakfast host Greg said: "If Radio 1 was a place, it would be Brighton.

"It's got an amazing musical heritage, loves bringing different people together and wants to make sure fun is prioritised.

"It's actually stupid that it's taken so long for us to do a Big Weekend there. Sorry about that."

EntertainmentTab.title: PETA protesters disrupt Sir Paul Smith's book talk
EntertainmentTab.text:
Fashion firm Paul Smith has told the BBC it is committed to animal welfare after protesters disrupted a talk by the brand's founder in his home city.

Two supporters of People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA) interrupted the event hosted by Sir Paul Smith at Nottingham's Broadway Cinema on Wednesday.

The protest follows investigations by PETA into alleged animal cruelty at mohair production facilities in South Africa and Lesotho, including one it said had links to a Paul Smith supplier.

The company said it upheld the highest standards of animal welfare across its supply chain.

The animal rights group said the pair were removed from the event by security.

In a statement, Elisa Allen, PETA's vice-president of programmes, said the brand had failed to act, prompting PETA to take its message directly to the man behind the label.

Mohair is a fibre made from the hair of Angora goats and is commonly used in clothing.

Smith said all its mohair was certified under the Responsible Mohair Standard (RMS) and that it would take relevant action if suppliers were found to be in breach of its animal welfare standards.

A spokesperson for Paul Smith said: "At Paul Smith, we uphold the highest standards of animal welfare across our supply chain, and all our suppliers are required to adhere to these standards.

"Every batch of mohair used by Paul Smith is certified to the Responsible Mohair Standard (RMS), the internationally recognised standard for responsible mohair production.

"If there is evidence that a supplier has not upheld these standards, we will take appropriate action in line with our ethical commitments."

PETA said its investigators had filmed goats being injured during shearing, including at mohair facilities under the RMS.

Allen said: "Hundreds of fashion brands have already ditched mohair, and Paul Smith must do the right thing and follow suit.

"PETA also urges shoppers to do their part by leaving cruelty on the rack and opting for animal-free materials such as cotton, hemp and bamboo."

Other brands, such as Helmut Lang, G-Star, Gap, Fred Perry, Barbour, UNIQLO, and Zara, have already banned mohair.
