EntertainmentTab.title: Gordon Ramsay to host Top Gear as show revived after Andrew Flintoff crash
EntertainmentTab.text:
TV chef Gordon Ramsay is to lead the new presenting line-up on BBC motoring show Top Gear, which is being revived four years after it was last on air.

Ramsay will take the driving seat alongside as yet unnamed co-presenters when the show starts filming next year. It will return to screens in 2028.

The long-running programme has been off air since 2022, when co-host Andrew Flintoff suffered serious facial and rib injuries after his open-topped three-wheeled car overturned at the show's test-track.

In a statement announcing his new role, Ramsay said he wants to bring "a fresh energy and ambition" to the show's formula of being "surprising, entertaining and [with] just the right amount of chaos".

Top Gear began in 1977 and became one of the BBC's biggest hits in the hands of Jeremy Clarkson, Richard Hammond and James May in the 2000s.

They were replaced by hosts including Chris Evans and Friends star Matt LeBlanc, before Flintoff took over in 2018 with Paddy McGuinness and Chris Harris.

But the show was "rested" after the former cricketer's crash in December 2022.

Flintoff was dragged face-down underneath the Morgan Super 3 car for about 50 metres. "I thought I was dead," he told a Disney+ documentary last year.

The BBC apologised and paid compensation to Flintoff following his crash.

In Wednesday's statement, Ramsay said he has had a love of cars since he grew up near the Silverstone race circuit in Northamptonshire.

"I would climb over the fences and sneak in for a glimpse of the racing," he said. "That early excitement sparked a lifelong passion for cars, motor sport, beautiful design and extraordinary engineering.

"At its very best Top Gear has always been about the unexpected - surprising, entertaining and just the right amount of chaos.

"That's the spirit we want to build on, bringing a fresh energy and ambition to create something truly thrilling for a whole new generation of audiences.

"It's an incredibly exciting opportunity, and I genuinely can't wait to get started!"

Former host Richard Hammond told BBC Radio 4's PM programme that Top Gear is "a grand old BBC stalwart".

"It goes back decades. We had our tenure of it and did our thing with it and went a bit crazy with it, and it'll be another incarnation of it," he said. "And great. It's a long runner, it'll carry on."

He said that he does not doubt Ramsay's credentials as a car fan, and joked that TV chefs "love three things: cooking - well in his case four - swearing, cooking, but also big watches and cars".

Hammond was seriously injured in a crash while filming the show in 2006, but said it "doesn't have to be" a dangerous show.

The BBC asked Hammond to return to the show for the new series, he said.

"They did talk to me about it. They came to me about maybe getting involved in leading the new Top Gear, and I don't want to drag it back to what it was. That's why I didn't do it," he said.

EntertainmentTab.title: Jesse Eisenberg says his films contain ‘no sexuality’. But maybe his fans are just less desperate?
EntertainmentTab.text:
The imminent arrival of Jesse Eisenberg’s new film The Debut should be cause for celebration. Not necessarily because it is good – although its star Julianne Moore seems locked into an Oscar nomination at minimum – but because it means that Jesse Eisenberg has to do press for it. This is always a treat.

While the bulk of big magazine profiles about film people involve journalists breaking their spines to make the subject sound funnier or more profound than they really are, that is never particularly necessary with Eisenberg, because he appears to be a genuine oddball.

For instance, the new profile about him in the New Yorker is brimming with endless weird little details that you would never expect to read in a piece about, say, Matt Damon. For example, he says that a Freudian analyst diagnosed him with something called “arousal disgust”, a complex where simply liking something brings about waves of self-hatred. He donated a kidney to a stranger. He wrote to the Directors Guild of America to ask that his name be taken off the opening titles of The Debut, not because he disowns it but because it felt needlessly flashy.

Aaron Sorkin, meanwhile – and you have to assume that this was meant as a compliment, compared Eisenberg to Holden Caulfield, the character who inspired Mark Chapman to murder John Lennon.

But by far the most interesting nugget from the profile concerns Eisenberg’s relationship with his fans. “People are mostly fine,” he says. “It’s because there’s no sexuality to my work. I think once the public is asked to want to sleep with a person onscreen, that person’s life is fundamentally different.”

This deserves some interrogation because, on the surface, it’s a statement that presents itself like a great unspoken truth. Of course there aren’t hordes of lusty fans pulling at his clothes all the time, because he doesn’t play the sort of character that attracts those people. If you are a leading man heart-throb like Leonardo DiCaprio, then you probably have to learn how to protect yourself from people who look at you like a randy cartoon wolf or, more specifically, Jeff Bezos’ wife.

But Jesse Eisenberg tends to make smaller films, where he plays superficially asexual characters. He’s very good at playing a child of divorce. He’s undeniably great at playing clever outsiders. And if we’re talking characters with no sexual magnetism whatsoever, you need to remember that Eisenberg repeatedly plays a stage magician in film.

However, some wider context is probably necessary. In the profile, Eisenberg was specifically talking about fans interrupting him when he’s writing, this is something he does during office hours at a New York public library branch. Immediately this means that we can narrow the focus a little, because it is clear that by “fans” he is describing a very narrow subsection of fans who happen to be visiting public libraries during weekday office hours. Not to generalise too broadly, but this doesn’t feel like a particularly sexually incontinent demographic.

And, besides, in terms of roles he has played, Eisenberg is just plain wrong. There is plenty of sexuality to his work. In Richard Ayoade’s adaptation of Dostoevsky’s The Double, he plays a twin who brims with sexual confidence throughout. In the series Fleishman is in Trouble, he plays a doctor who has so much casual sex post-divorce that it has to be condensed into a montage. And in the play The Spoils – which Eisenberg wrote for himself a decade ago – his character admits to having scatological fantasies about his friend’s girlfriend.

Most damningly of all, there is the very famous interview he did with Romina Puga in 2013, which is one of the most sexually charged things you will ever clap eyes on. From start to finish, the interview is a cavalcade of flirtatious bullying in both directions, like they’re determined to neg each other into bed. Of course, we should remember that Eisenberg was a bit too relentless in this regard, and in a subsequent post entitled “Jesse Eisenberg isn’t very nice”, she describes how the encounter left her feeling humiliated.

But still, it blows a hole clean through Eisenberg’s argument. People aren’t nice to him because he isn’t sexual in movies, they’re nice to him because he makes small, clever films enjoyed primarily by people who are too shy to barge in on him when he’s clearly working in a library on a Thursday. Now, let this be the end of it, because I don’t want to convince Jesse Eisenberg that people fancy him any more than I absolutely have to.

GeneralTab.title: Huntingdon train attack survivor praises man who saved her during stabbings
GeneralTab.text:
A student who survived the Huntingdon train attack has met for the first time with the passenger she believes saved her life during the stabbings.

Astrid told BBC News that Stephen Crean's decision to confront Anthony Williams gave her time to escape. "I owe him my life," she said.

Williams was found guilty on Thursday of attempting to murder Crean and 13 others.

The then 19-year-old and 61-year-old Crean were just strangers on a train when she ran down the carriage screaming that there was a man with a knife.

Passengers on the Doncaster to King's Cross service fought off Williams, 33, with a frying pan and a toaster as the attack unfolded on 1 November 2025.

Crean ran towards Williams and was stabbed in the hands, back and neck. She was the last person to reach the buffet car and believes his actions gave her time to get in and shut the door.

Meeting after the guilty verdicts were delivered, the two train passengers hugged.

Astrid told the Nottingham Forest fan, who had been travelling home from a match: "It's brilliant to meet you... now we will know each other for a long time."

Crean said: "It means the world to me to meet her. Meeting her was the best thing, it was worth waiting for. I'm just so happy."

Astrid, who did not want to use her last name, said Crean was a hero for his actions that day.

"I just owe him everything," she said, before adding: "I wouldn't be here today without you, and to put your life on the line for someone else, a complete stranger, is just complete bravery."

She said Crean had a "split second to make a decision" and she owed him her life because of that.

"So I'd just like to say thank you," she said.

Crean praised her for alerting him to the danger of Williams as she ran past.

"You can be proud of yourself, and your parents will be proud of you," he added.

During the trial, Crean told the court he decided "to try to stop" the attack and "launched himself towards and at" Williams.

Crean and Astrid both faced terrifying moments as Williams rampaged down the train.

Crean said Williams asked, "Do you want to die?" as he stabbed him several times.

Crean then managed to lock himself in a toilet and call 999 telling them what had happened and that he was covered in blood and scared.

He said he remembered seeing Astrid crying with makeup running down her face.

The fashion student said she remembered seeing Crean throw himself at the attacker and put himself between her and Williams so she could escape.

"I was able to shut the door with the rest of the people behind me. If you hadn't been in between us... I have no idea what would have happened if you weren't there, literally in that second."

Astrid had seen an interview with the 62-year-old on the BBC two days after the attack and contacted the BBC to say he was the man on the train who had helped protect her and others.

Only now the trial has finished have they been able to meet.

Crean said he is pleased the jury found Williams guilty of attempting to murder him as he did not believe he should be allowed to get away with the vicious attacks on him and the other passengers.

On Thursday Cambridgeshire police apologised for failings in stopping Williams after another stabbing the month before the Huntingdon attack.

As well as the train attacks, Williams was found guilty of attempting to murder four other people in separate incidents and will be sentenced at Cambridge Crown Court on 4 and 5 February.

Crean believes more should have been done to prevent these further offences. "I think they should have had him before. He shouldn't have been allowed to go running around like this. And if they'd picked up on it, we'd have had him before."

Having survived the attack, Astrid is running the London marathon for Crimestoppers as part of her efforts to turn around the harrowing situation she found herself in.

She can, she says, because of Stephen Crean's actions. And he has promised to be there for her again: this time on the finish line.

GeneralTab.title: Zelensky tells BBC US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough
GeneralTab.text:
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles are costing Ukrainian lives and complaining that the US is not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks.

In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president also said it was "strange" that Donald Trump had posted a photo of himself embracing Vladimir Putin as "my friend".

"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.

"He's an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.

Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States.

Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.

The latest round of peace talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.

He said talks were expected to resume in December.

On Thursday, Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".

But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.

And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.

The Kremlin appears to be resisting.

Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.

Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.

So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".

"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.

The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.

In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.

The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.

Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.

Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.

But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Americans were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.

"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.

"The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."

He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink – and its military version, Starshield – were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.

Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.

So whose decision was that?

"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."

GeneralTab.title: Tebbutt attack in Lamu: Kenyan Ali Kololo says Met Police ruined his life
GeneralTab.text:
A Kenyan woodcutter who was wrongly convicted and sentenced to death over an attack on a British couple has told the BBC that actions by London's Metropolitan Police involved in the case destroyed his life.

Somali gunmen broke into David and Judith Tebbutt's beach bungalow on the Kenyan coast in 2011. They shot David dead and abducted Judith, holding her captive in Somalia for six months.

Met detectives flew to Kenya to assist the investigation. Their evidence helped convict Ali Kololo, who spent more than a decade in prison before his conviction was overturned.

Kololo is suing the Met, claiming a senior officer, former Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, gave misleading evidence at his trial and acted unlawfully to secure his conviction.

In his first media interview, he told the BBC about his 15-year ordeal and his fight for compensation, which the Met is challenging in court.

We meet on Lamu, a small island off Kenya's northern coast, once a thriving Swahili port. People and goods are still carted through its narrow stone streets by donkey rather than car.

It was here, in 2013, that Kololo was sentenced to death.

Standing at the jetty, where police once brought him ashore in handcuffs, he relishes being free. But he is struggling to rebuild his life.

"Everything was taken from me. I'm starting from zero. I don't think I'll ever go back to who I was before," he says.

Before his arrest, Kololo lived with his wife and their three young children. He had once worked as a groundskeeper at the resort where the Tebbutts were staying, but by 2011 he earned his living felling trees in a local forest and selling the wood.

"My life was very good," he says. "I was fending for myself, taking good care of my family."

Within 24 hours of the attack, Kenyan police had arrested him.

"I was beaten with clubs and thrown into a car," he says. "They beat me for days, burning me with cigarettes, forcing me to confess to things. They subjected me to torture like no other."

Kololo could not read or write. He says police made him put his thumbprint on a statement claiming he had led the attackers to the Tebbutts.

"I didn't understand anything," he says, calling the statement "a mountain of lies". "I signed it without knowing what it was because of the state they had put me in".

The Kenyan police told us it "at all times strives to work within the law". Kololo is not suing them.

Within days of the attack, a team of Met officers, led by then Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, arrived to support the Kenyan investigation. The UK government had instructed the officers not to accept information from the Kenyan authorities that had been obtained by interrogating detainees.

But Hibberd requested Kololo's statement and later relied on it when giving evidence for the prosecution at his trial.

In court, Hibberd also presented evidence linking Kololo to the attack. He told the Kenyan court Kololo had been wearing a type of shoe that matched footwear marks found in the sand at the resort.

The officer who had arrested Kololo said he was barefoot when he was handed to police. Hibberd did not disclose that the Met's own forensic examination could not establish whether the shoe in question had made the marks.

At the trial, Kololo did not initially have a lawyer. He had to cross-examine all the prosecution witnesses himself, including Hibberd, through an interpreter who spoke Swahili, which was not Kololo's first language.

"I believe I was framed because I am a poor man and I did not have the strength or means to fight for myself," Kololo says.

Kololo was convicted of kidnap and robbery with violence - the only person ever convicted in connection with the attack. He spent three years on death row before his sentence was commuted to life imprisonment.

He recalls seeing his prison file. In the space for the expiry date, someone had written "death".

"I was completely heartbroken. I believed I could be executed at any moment, and I would never see my family, my children, ever again."

Years later, the UK's Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) established that Hibberd had omitted significant forensic evidence at the trial. It found that he would have had a case to answer for gross misconduct, but he could not face disciplinary proceedings because he had retired from the force. At the time, his lawyer said Hibberd absolutely disagreed with the report's findings.

In April 2023, Kenya's High Court quashed Kololo's conviction, because of doubts over the prosecution's evidence. This followed years of work by the legal charity Reprieve and a Kenyan lawyer, Alfred Olaba, who represented him for free.

They were supported by Judith Tebbutt, who believed Kololo was innocent. In an interview with the BBC in 2022, she said he had been scapegoated by Scotland Yard.

"He was not there on the night. He was not part of the group that held me. They've put this man in prison without any real evidence."

More than three years after his release, Kololo says he is still living with the effects of his torture and decade in prison. As we walk the narrow streets of Lamu's old town, his thin frame moves stiffly. He is on edge. "My mind is not good," he says. "I have not recovered."

He remembers being kept in a filthy, bedbug-ridden cell with up to eight other inmates, which he thought he would never leave. Twice he contracted tuberculosis and nearly died.

Kololo is now too frail to do the woodcutting he once relied on to make a living. He tries to grow enough to eat on the land around his home, but erratic rain makes it difficult.

"I have nothing. On the days I get food, I eat, and on the days I don't, I endure."

He lives alone in a mud hut. His wife divorced him after he went to prison, and their children went to live with his mother. They dropped out of school because the family could not pay the fees. Kololo says they were not allowed to visit him in prison. When he was released, they barely remembered him, especially his youngest.

"They were too young. Only now are they starting to regain the memory that 'this is our father who disappeared'," he says. "If it weren't for my mother, my children might have died."

For much of our time together, Kololo is remarkably upbeat. He trusts that his lawyers and God will deliver him justice. But when we talk about the Met, his demeanour shifts.

"I am extremely angry with the police," he says. "I'm also angry with the Kenyan Police. They collaborated to incriminate me. What [Hibberd] said destroyed my entire life and my children's lives."

The Met has not apologised to Kololo or admitted wrongdoing. The force is contesting his compensation claim, which his lawyers say could take years to resolve.

"These people falsely accused me. Do I not deserve something?" he asks.

The Met told the BBC that neither they nor Hibberd wanted to comment on Kololo's claim, but it said: "Our thoughts are with Mr Kololo, Mrs Tebbutt, her family and all those who have been affected by this terrible crime. The Metropolitan Police remains committed to supporting the Kenyan authorities in any way that may be possible, in order to get justice for Mrs Tebbutt and her late husband."

Preetha Gopalan, Reprieve's head of UK litigation, describes the Met's behaviour in Kololo's case as "egregious".

"They've spent 10 years trying to evade accountability in every way possible, now dragging him through the courts," she says. "It's possible for them to do the right thing, but they are unwilling, and so this ordeal continues to haunt Kololo and his family."

"Even if I get a billion shillings, I will never be the same," Kololo says. "But if I get the justice I deserve, I can help my children and take care of myself when I am an old man."

GeneralTab.title: Why Trump's new tariffs are less of a threat
GeneralTab.text:
There was none of last April's fanfare, the Rose Garden reveal, the gameshow blue board or "Liberation Day" rhetoric surrounding Trump's tariff announcement this week.

Instead there is something rather tentative about this latest exercise with talk of further negotiations.

"We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC.

Around the world the view is that this week's announcement is an attempt to shore up the domestic legal underpinning of these tariffs, more than a fundamental change in the Trump trade agenda.

The tariffs are also not due to come in until January or possibly February, after a period of consultation. There has already been eight months of process and hearings, and the rates announced are upper ceilings, often up for negotiation. It's quite the contrast to the overnight shock meted out to the world last April.

Still, the US is making the argument that large swathes of the rest of the world, including allies, are harming the US goods trade position by supporting their own industries. This is the basis for the tariffs, in large part replacing the previous tariffs justified on "forced labour" provisions.

The UK, which was unaffected by the new tariff announcements, remains caught by the forced labour provisions, albeit at a rate of 10% extra on global tariffs. There was no move in response to the UK's digital services tax.

It means for many important countries there are now two legal bases upon which the Trump tariffs rest, after the Supreme Court struck down the original emergency basis earlier this year. A group of 25 states has taken the Trump administration to court to strike down the forced labour tariffs.

The tariffs will have to be finalised under a Democrat Congress, which has influence, but not power. The Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries said this week that the new House would in its first 100 days "move aggressively to… repeal the Trump tariffs".

The Chinese rate of 20% is the truce rate from last year's Trump-Xi deal. The truce is due to expire in mid-January. Beijing's response was muted, no retaliation, criticism of industrial overcapacity as a "false issue", and a call to implement the Xi-Trump deal. The leverage over China has weakened, with the US share of its exports dropping to around 10% this year, down from 15%, just two years ago, and 19% in 2018.

GeneralTab.title: I spend £200 a month on fancy meals by myself - would you dine solo?
GeneralTab.text:
Catherine Smith is perusing the menu at a high-end Mediterranean restaurantshe has been excited to try. She has a new outfit on, and as she sips her rosé, shelooks across at the empty seat - bliss.

"I think what is so special about solo dining is that you don't have to wait for people to make those plans. You can go out and do them yourself," says the 23-year-old.

The self-confessed foodie is part of a growing trend of people booking tables for one - not because they're away with work but as a treat.

As food trends analyst Charles Banks puts it: "[Eating alone] is becoming an intentional act, a little pocket of independence, indulgence and self-care."

We spoke to solo dining fans and hospitality industry experts about how the trend is shaping the restaurant experience and asked if you would book a table for one.

Catherine, from Yorkshire, began dining solo at university and now does it at least once a month, choosing high-end restaurants she would not usually go to with friends and family.

She has been to a range of places both in the UK and abroad, doing "lots of research" to find new spots, typically spending £100 to £200 per meal.

"I think because a lot of my friends are vegan or vegetarian, I find that difficult sometimes because I'm quite a big meat eater," she says.

"I find it nice to be able to go out and pick a restaurant where I haven't had to scour through the menu to make sure that it's suitable for them."

Catherine says the sense of freedom she gets from picking where and when she eats "feels empowering".

"It definitely feels like not only a form of self-care but also a form of female liberation."

Online booking platform OpenTable says it covers more than 5,000 restaurants in the UK. It says solo dining makes up the smallest proportion of its bookings in the UK but it is the fastest-growing category.

Figures from 1 January to 31 August this year saw a rise of 23% in solo bookings compared to the same time period a year ago. It did not provide the data to the BBC to verify.

Nishi Singh was an avid solo diner when she lived in London, but found it wasn't widely accepted after moving to Delhi.

"Someone approached me and said that they assumed I'd been stood up," she tells BBC World Service's The Food Chain podcast.

"It sparked a conversation about the culture around solo dining in Delhi and I was really shocked to hear that it's not really something people do."

A couple of days later, she started documenting her solo dining experience on social media.

"Quite a lot of people have reached out and said that this is something they'd like to do and they're too scared to do it themselves," she says.

However, some restaurants like Jungli, an Indian restaurant in Newcastle upon Tyne, is working to attract solo diners.

Co-founder and director Yousaf Khalid has included high tables and bar seats in his recently opened restaurant. They also have charging points for laptops and phones.

"We want people to feel comfortable in these sorts of environments, being able to walk in on their own," he says.

He has hired staff with "bigger personalities" to engage customers in conversation but they also know when to leave diners alone if they want a more solitary experience.

Catherine urges anyone who fancies solo dining to give it a go.

"Food is a great way to bring people together, but it's also a great way to have good experiences on your own.

"I think with time, people will see and will start to accept it as something that's more normal."

Additional reporting by Jemma Crew and Emma Jackson.

articles.title: Huntingdon train attack survivor praises man who saved her during stabbings
articles.text:
A student who survived the Huntingdon train attack has met for the first time with the passenger she believes saved her life during the stabbings.

Astrid told BBC News that Stephen Crean's decision to confront Anthony Williams gave her time to escape. "I owe him my life," she said.

Williams was found guilty on Thursday of attempting to murder Crean and 13 others.

The then 19-year-old and 61-year-old Crean were just strangers on a train when she ran down the carriage screaming that there was a man with a knife.

Passengers on the Doncaster to King's Cross service fought off Williams, 33, with a frying pan and a toaster as the attack unfolded on 1 November 2025.

Crean ran towards Williams and was stabbed in the hands, back and neck. She was the last person to reach the buffet car and believes his actions gave her time to get in and shut the door.

Meeting after the guilty verdicts were delivered, the two train passengers hugged.

Astrid told the Nottingham Forest fan, who had been travelling home from a match: "It's brilliant to meet you... now we will know each other for a long time."

Crean said: "It means the world to me to meet her. Meeting her was the best thing, it was worth waiting for. I'm just so happy."

Astrid, who did not want to use her last name, said Crean was a hero for his actions that day.

"I just owe him everything," she said, before adding: "I wouldn't be here today without you, and to put your life on the line for someone else, a complete stranger, is just complete bravery."

She said Crean had a "split second to make a decision" and she owed him her life because of that.

"So I'd just like to say thank you," she said.

Crean praised her for alerting him to the danger of Williams as she ran past.

"You can be proud of yourself, and your parents will be proud of you," he added.

During the trial, Crean told the court he decided "to try to stop" the attack and "launched himself towards and at" Williams.

Crean and Astrid both faced terrifying moments as Williams rampaged down the train.

Crean said Williams asked, "Do you want to die?" as he stabbed him several times.

Crean then managed to lock himself in a toilet and call 999 telling them what had happened and that he was covered in blood and scared.

He said he remembered seeing Astrid crying with makeup running down her face.

The fashion student said she remembered seeing Crean throw himself at the attacker and put himself between her and Williams so she could escape.

"I was able to shut the door with the rest of the people behind me. If you hadn't been in between us... I have no idea what would have happened if you weren't there, literally in that second."

Astrid had seen an interview with the 62-year-old on the BBC two days after the attack and contacted the BBC to say he was the man on the train who had helped protect her and others.

Only now the trial has finished have they been able to meet.

Crean said he is pleased the jury found Williams guilty of attempting to murder him as he did not believe he should be allowed to get away with the vicious attacks on him and the other passengers.

On Thursday Cambridgeshire police apologised for failings in stopping Williams after another stabbing the month before the Huntingdon attack.

As well as the train attacks, Williams was found guilty of attempting to murder four other people in separate incidents and will be sentenced at Cambridge Crown Court on 4 and 5 February.

Crean believes more should have been done to prevent these further offences. "I think they should have had him before. He shouldn't have been allowed to go running around like this. And if they'd picked up on it, we'd have had him before."

Having survived the attack, Astrid is running the London marathon for Crimestoppers as part of her efforts to turn around the harrowing situation she found herself in.

She can, she says, because of Stephen Crean's actions. And he has promised to be there for her again: this time on the finish line.

articles.title: Zelensky tells BBC US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough
articles.text:
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles are costing Ukrainian lives and complaining that the US is not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks.

In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president also said it was "strange" that Donald Trump had posted a photo of himself embracing Vladimir Putin as "my friend".

"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.

"He's an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.

Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States.

Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.

The latest round of peace talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.

He said talks were expected to resume in December.

On Thursday, Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".

But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.

And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.

The Kremlin appears to be resisting.

Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.

Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.

So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".

"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.

The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.

In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.

The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.

Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.

Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.

But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Americans were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.

"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.

"The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."

He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink – and its military version, Starshield – were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.

Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.

So whose decision was that?

"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."

articles.title: UK to pay 'participation' fee to deliver EU deals
articles.text:
The UK will pay a "participation fee" to the EU as part of the deals agreed by Andy Burnham, according to legal documents.

The surcharge will go towards the running costs of EU agencies and systems required to deliver two of the agreements unveiled by the prime minister last week.

It will be paid in addition to a contribution towards costs that broadly mirrors how EU members contribute to the bloc's shared budget, the documents show.

The government has sought to contrast the financial costs of the deals against their overall effect on the economy, which it estimates will receive an eventual boost by billions a year due to increased trade.

The government is yet to publish an estimate of overall additional costs, but officials said they expected them to be in the low tens of millions per year and "massively outweighed" by predicted economic gains.

British ministers had already said they were prepared to pay towards administrative costs required to implement deals to re-link the UK to the EU's carbon trading regime, and align Britain with the EU's food standards.

Now, details of how the payments will be calculated have been revealed in treaties to deliver the two agreements, which are meant to take effect during 2028.

Legal text for a third agreement agreed last week, on youth visas for 18 to 31 year olds, is expected to be published in the coming days.

According to the treaties, the payments will be made as a share of the running costs of three EU agencies, as well as various systems that will be used to implement the food standards and emissions deals.

The bulk of the payments, to be made in euros, will come in the form of an "operational contribution" in proportion to the size of the British economy compared to that of the EU.

This broadly mirrors the way in which EU member states split the cost of their main contributions towards the bloc's overall budget.

But in addition, the UK will also pay a "participation fee" set at 4% of its main contribution figure.

The government has pointed to the 2021 Brexit trade agreement negotiated by the Conservatives, which also applied an additional surcharge to UK contributions towards the cost of relevant EU programmes.

However, any additional contributions are likely to be seized upon by opponents of the latest deals.

Ministers had declined to enter into specifics of the fees during negotiations on the treaties. On Sunday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the latest deals agreed by Burnham were "not about cost to the taxpayer".

It comes as the government published separate legislation granting it broad powers to incorporate new EU laws required to implement the agreements, without having to hold a full vote each time.

The food standards deal in particular will mean Britain will have to align with scores of current EU food-related laws that have been updated since Brexit, along with future rules in these areas.

The government argues the new powers are required because it would be impractical to run a full parliamentary process each time UK legislation needs to be updated to make the agreement work.

But it has prompted criticism from opposition parties, because the UK no longer has voting rights at the EU to shape European legislation.

The government argues the UK will get a say on new rules, with the treaty texts confirming British experts can be consulted when new EU laws are being drawn up, with the UK granted "observer" status in certain meetings.

But Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Burnham was showing "disdain for the democratic process" by asking for a "blank cheque to install and enact EU law".

"The prime minister is telling MPs to hand him extraordinary powers whilst having no idea what the EU will actually agree to," she added.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has argued the Burnham's deals would take Britain back into "much of the European Union's single market".

He added: "European economies are not growing as fast as ours. The idea that getting closer to the EU will mean growth for us is a myth."

articles.title: 'Horrible spike' in flu warning as hospital admissions surge
articles.text:
A surge in severe cases of flu has prompted health officials in England to urge those most at risk to get vaccinated as soon as possible.

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said hospital admission rates had soared by almost 80% over the last week to the highest at this time of year since before the Covid pandemic.

Flu vaccine uptake so far among those aged 65 and over was just under 68% - lower than where it usually was at this time of year, the agency said. The flu can be very serious for those living with some long-term health conditions.

Outgoing chief executive for NHS England, Sir Jim Mackey, talked of how some hospitals had introduced mask-wearing to stem the spread of respiratory illnesses.

Speaking at the NHS Alliance autumn conference, Sir Jim said he was asked to wear a mask for the first time in years during a hospital visit, saying it was "a bit of a shock".

"I think we have more beds occupied with flu than we did this time last year, as we're just about going to that horrible spike in flu," he said.

According to the UKHSA, almost 9.5 million people under the age of 65 in clinical risk groups - including those with lung conditions, kidney or liver disease and diabetes - are eligible for the flu jab.

However, only 34% had received a flu vaccine up to 22 November, leaving almost 7 million without vital protection.

Sir Jim also condemned corridor care in hospitals saying that it had become "embedded" in some parts of the health service.

"It's not something any of us would want for our families, our mothers, our aunties, uncles – whether it's from a safety point of view, or more importantly from a personal dignity point of view," he said, adding there was a need to get a grip and eliminate it.

Sir Ciaran Devane, chief executive of the NHS Alliance, representing employers, said: "While the flu season is clearly hitting earlier this year and could add to the strain on NHS services heading into another difficult winter, we are yet to see how or when it will peak.

"The NHS has already had to deal with the challenge of heatwaves this summer, so this could pile yet more pressure on already squeezed services."

UKHSA flu lead Dr Suzanna McDonald urged people to get vaccinated, saying thousands of people die from the flu every year.

Flu levels are expected to increase further as Christmas approaches and people start socialising indoors more.

McDonald also called on those who are ill with respiratory symptoms to practise good hand hygiene by washing hands with warm soapy water, cough and sneeze into elbow or into a tissue, and to stay at home in bed and avoid anyone at much higher risk from catching diseases.

Meanwhile, it emerged that just a little over a third of toddlers in England have had a vaccine so far this autumn on the NHS.

Two and three-year-olds can have the vaccine, given as a nasal spray, for free at pharmacies.

But the UKHSA said just 37% of those eligible had taken up the offer.

School age children usually have the vaccine at school, with a catch-up available in pharmacies until 1 December for those who missed it.

McDonald said: "Please don't dismiss the importance of a flu vaccine for your children.

"It will help keep them out of hospital and even save lives."

This time last year an early increase in flu cases caused real concern across the NHS.

The virus was spreading sooner than expected and the fear was that the numbers would continue climbing right through the always challenging Christmas and New Year period.

As it happened the outbreak peaked early and the bleakest predictions did not become reality.

This time hospital admissions with flu patients are a little higher than 12 months ago after another early surge materialised.

Once again, officials do not know when the peak might be reached.

Adding to the challenges is an increase over the last year in patient numbers with a range of illnesses and conditions, partly explained by the ageing population. That means even more pressure on hospitals and their staff.

A bad flu winter could create significant problems.

articles.title: Leaders clash in final Spain election debate as housing dominates run-in
articles.text:
Spain's main party leaders have made their last pitch to voters in a fractious final TV debate that focused heavily on the country's housing crisis.

Spaniards go to the ballot box on Sunday, with opinion polls suggesting Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez will fail to extend his eight years in office.

The debate on Thursday night marked the culmination of a campaign, which has been defined by the din of house keys being jangled in symbolic protest, rather than any carefully crafted words of politicians.

The struggle many face in opening the door to an affordable home has led to demonstrations filling plazas across the country.

Alberto Núñez Feijóo of the conservative People's Party (PP), who is poised to replace Sánchez, told viewers he would build a million new homes.

PP, which is narrowly projected to be the largest party, is poised to form a government with the far-right Vox party which is polling in third place.

This would be the first time the far right has assumed power at the national level in Spain's 50 years of democracy following the Franco dictatorship.

Vox's leader Santiago Abascal told the debate only he cared about those who had the greatest housing need.

Ada Colau, who heads a left-wing coalition of four small left-wing parties called Broad Front, said taxing rich and exploitative landlords was urgently required.

Rejecting criticism that he had failed to tackle the country's housing problem, Sanchez talked up his recent emergency measures designed to protect tenants and cap rents.

Sparking the protests in September was the eviction – and subsequent death in hospital – of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal (no relation to Santiago). She could not afford a tripling of her rent in Madrid.

But it is Spain's third city, Valencia, that is at the heart of what many call a full-blown housing crisis.

"We want to live together but we look at the prices of property and it's impossible," says 25-year-old Nuria Cifuentes from the city.

She and her boyfriend Miguel Martínez work as sports journalists but are still living with their respective families because of the high cost of renting a flat, even with their combined salaries.

"Half of what we earn would go on rent of more than 1,000 euros a month," Miguel, 26, says.

We meet the couple outside Valencia's futuristic science museum, whose distinctive design is often compared to the skeleton of a whale.

This coastal location has witnessed the biggest rise in rent prices of any major Spanish city over the past half a decade, according to official data from the INE, the national statistics office.

One study from the city's Polytechnic University put the increase at 78% between 2020 and 2025.

Sánchez called a snap election after Congress rejected his emergency housing reforms.

A revised version was later pushed through a parliamentary standing committee – restricting evictions and capping rent rises – but opponents say he has had eight years to sort the problem and has resolutely failed.

Nuria and Miguel say the soaring cost of housing means that life is on pause for them, as they're unable to make concrete plans for the future.

"Maybe we want to have kids, maybe we want to actually buy somewhere, but there are so many unknowns that all I see is a black expanse," Nuria says.

"The problem here is that our salaries are very low and life is very expensive."

The wider cost of living is the second most important issue for Spaniards, according to numerous surveys carried out during this election period.

Wages failing to catch up with rising prices – despite Spain's GDP growing faster than the three bigger EU countries, Germany, France and Italy – is another reason why Sánchez's PSOE party is only sitting in second place, according to final opinion polls.

Feijóo is said to be most likely to form the next government with the support of the far-right Vox under its leader Santiago Abascal.

Having called access to housing a "vital emergency", Feijóo wants to cut taxes for under-40s buying their first home and scrap the Socialists' housing law.

Opponents of Vox say those who have arrived legally and live and work peacefully risk being forced out.

But 30-year-old Daniel, who is currently unemployed, says he is ready to give his vote to Vox for the first time.

"First of all, it's immigration. It's bad in Spain today – that's why I'm going further to the right," he says.

"The left helps those who don't work, but we need people who work and contribute. We need to give less aid to people who come from abroad and don't contribute."

Daniel says taxes need to come down immediately.

"We are almost being charged to just breathe at the moment," he says.

We meet Daniel coming out of a shopping centre. We explain that other people we met in the previous hour who told us they support Vox did not want to give their name or be photographed.

Is he proud to be voting far right, or does he have concerns about his choice?

"I'll say it like it is… I've always been centre right but have gone to the extreme right… I've decided to choose nationalism."

Spain's control of its borders was criticised by 22 of its 26 EU partners in the summer, in a rebuke to Sánchez.

In July more than 70,000 migrants crossed into the Spanish territory of Ceuta in just two days.

Vox called it an "invasion".

Sánchez has argued the foreign workforce is essential to Spain's economic growth, and in April announced plans to give half a million undocumented migrants legal status.

In the final days of the campaign, Sánchez has made a flurry of new spending announcements amounting to billions of euros, promising wage rises in the public sector, higher pensions and discounted transport.

Twenty-year-old student María García says she welcomes the promises but asks why they have come so late in the day.

"The Socialist party have been in power for eight years and now suddenly, during the election campaign, they are passing a lot of progressive laws – which I agree with – but isn't that hypocritical?" she says.

"I don't really have a choice but to vote for them, but come on – you had eight years to do all this!"

Maria's sentiments chime with those of her boyfriend German Martinez, 18.

I put it to them that nearly a fifth of Spaniards are said to be choosing Vox and a number of studies say it's set to be the top choice of first-time voters.

María shakes her head.

"I believe Spain is stepping into the lion's den because we are scared of the dogs outside. We need to be careful," she says.

"People need to inform themselves – just listen to what these guys say. That 20% of Spanish people agree with them really scares me."

Sánchez will be hoping that fear among the undecided of a national government that includes Vox will save him.

He is a great political survivor, but even if his party wins the most votes he has no obvious path to build a majority.

The man who called a snap election over housing now faces his own eviction - from office.

articles.title: Chris Mason: Immigration stats are down but will that be the end of the issue?
articles.text:
Net migration falling to the tens of thousands is a landmark moment in our collective national conversation about immigration over the last couple of decades.

There is a simple reason for this. We have had years and years strewn with the litter of politicians promising to cut net migration to under 100,000 annually.

But it never happened, until now.

In the latter decades of the last century, net migration was broadly net zero. Sometimes more folk left than arrived. But, around the time that I first arrived as a reporter in Westminster in 2004, the story was changing and would change rapidly.

I have followed every twist, turn, argument and campaign since, both from Parliament and from Brussels.

On 1 May 2004, the European Union expanded hugely, from 15 to 25 members, the biggest expansion in its history.

The bloc's population grew by 74 million people overnight as countries including Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Slovakia, Slovenia and what was then the Czech Republic signed up.

And remember, a core plank of EU membership is freedom of movement: the right to travel, live and work anywhere in the club.

Transitional controls on workers from these former communist states could be applied at the time, but the then-Labour government led by Tony Blair chose not to.

The consequences of that decision were as substantial as they were consequential.

Ministers had predicted a minimal impact. But net migration cranked up.

Crucially, this began to ground arguments about sovereignty in the swirling debates about the UK's membership of the EU.

At the time I was a Europe correspondent based in Brussels and a frequent visitor to the European Parliament in Strasbourg.

The UK Independence Party, led by Nigel Farage, were on the rise. But Eurosceptics would tell me privately that their deeply held concerns about the loss of sovereignty, of power, to EU institutions had been a hard sell to many back home. It was an argument, regardless of its merits or otherwise, that felt theoretical and intellectual to many, rather than practical and grounded in day-to-day concerns.

But that changed for many given the scale of immigration people could see.

Plenty of places, particularly beyond the big cities, felt the rapidity of change. Immigration took on a greater political salience.

Should all control over migration be re-imported to Westminster? Such was the growing strength of feeling among many, a sequence of prime ministers began promising to reduce net migration to the tens of thousands.

David Cameron made the promise. The Conservative election manifesto in 2010 harked back to those numbers before the turn of the century. "We will take steps to take net migration back to the levels of the 1990s – tens of thousands a year, not hundreds of thousands."

Five years later, Cameron renewed the promise, in the Conservative manifesto of 2015. The party would "keep our ambition of delivering annual net migration in the tens of thousands, not the hundreds of thousands," it read.

By 2017, Theresa May was prime minister and while the UK had voted for Brexit, it hadn't happened yet. In the Conservative manifesto that year, she promised "controlled, sustainable migration, with net migration down to the tens of thousands."

At the 2019 general election, Boris Johnson was in Downing Street. He didn't repeat the tens of thousands promise, post Brexit, instead arguing for an "Australian-style points-based immigration system" and, crucially, that "overall numbers will come down."

They didn't. Instead, they soared by almost a million – a giant spike on the graph of recent net migration, branded by his critics as the "Boriswave."

Johnson argued that Brexit would mean Westminster would take back control of migration, as leaving the European Union would mean the end of freedom of movement among the member states.

And yes, Brexit did repatriate that power. But this delivered choices, not a guaranteed outcome that the numbers would fall. And Johnson's choices led instead to a spectacular rise.

It took Rishi Sunak's government and the then-Home Secretary Sir James Cleverly to substantially change the rules and so limit the number of visas granted. The incoming Labour government in 2024 inherited these rules and kept them.

The question now, with the net migration number now in the tens of thousands, is whether immigration will now shrivel as a topic of widespread worry.

How migration feels can be influenced by world view and wealth, politics and geography. Let's take just one aspect of it: the number of asylum seekers being housed in Scotland has increased by 20% over the past year, despite a fall in numbers across the UK as a whole. Glasgow remains the council area with the largest number of people in asylum accommodation in the UK, and there have been increases in areas from Aberdeen to North Lanarkshire which buck the UK-wide trend.

And a lower net figure also does not necessarily mean that the scale of immigration and emigration are low. Large but similar numbers merely serve to almost cancel each other out, numerically. The underlying official statistics set out that an estimated 738,000 people immigrated to the UK in the year to June, while 661,000 emigrated.

But just as previous political choices still have consequences now, a persistently low net migration number, depending on who is coming and going, could have consequences in the future. Take Andy Burnham's desire to shake up social care in England, a sector traditionally reliant on arrivals from overseas for much of its workforce. How might it cope? It's one of many potential questions for the future.

For now, as we examine this latest set of statistics, many will reflect that we have collectively as a country – if not everyone individually - exuded an anguish, sometimes an anger at the scale of immigration. It has been one of the standout demographic, social and so political issues of recent times. Perhaps now that conversation turns to a new chapter.

articles.title: MoD has no email addresses for about half of its reservists
articles.text:
The Ministry of Defence (MoD) is urging reservists to update their contact details, after it has emerged it does not have email addresses for about half of them.

The UK has an estimated 95,000 members in its strategic reserve force, which is made up of veterans who can be recalled in exceptional circumstances, but the MoD said it has only been able to send letters to around 50,000.

Open letters have been published on the ministry's website encouraging others to "reconnect".

On Thursday Defence Secretary Wes Streeting confirmed that the MoD had written to ex-military personnel to check their contact details and skills against the backdrop of a rising "threat environment".

His comments were made after The Times and the Telegraph reported that reservists who previously served in the Armed Forces had received letters telling them to prepare to be called up for war.

Streeting told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that this meant should they ever be needed "either for a national disaster here at home or for a more serious threat or conflict elsewhere" then they would "know where our strategic reserve is" and what their skills were.

"I want the country to be alert, not alarmed," he said.

The defence secretary also reiterated the importance of keeping "up to date" with reservists, and ensuring they had access to "further development opportunities".

On the MoD's website, the ministry said it was re-engaging with reservists due to a "more dangerous and unpredictable security environment."

It emphasised that the threshold for being recalled is high and reservists would not be used to fill routine staffing shortages in peacetime.

"It may be considered for serious national emergencies, warlike operations, preparations for war or a major crisis that requires additional military capability," it said.

Earlier this year, former Defence Secretary Lord Robertson said officials were failing to maintain records of military veterans who were entering the reserves.

"The Ministry of Defence at the present moment doesn't even know where most of them are," he said in April.

"So we need to round up those who are available and fit and willing to be able to do it."

Air Chief Marshal Sir Richard Knighton has made similar comments, warning in January that the UK did not have "an effective system of tracking and engaging" personnel after they had left the Armed Forces.

articles.title: The young hikers finding friendship and fresh air offline
articles.text:
After years toiling all day at a desk as an aerospace engineer in Istanbul, 26-year-old Mohannad Najjar decided to swap his screen for a degree in nature and theology in Cambridge and a volunteering gig as a scout leader.

He walks in the countryside every weekend and has hiked in wild locations in the Scottish Highlands, which he credits with helping him think clearly.

"I just want to see something that's untouched, to be in nature," he says. "When you come in from a hike or a walk, you just feel different."

Najjar is one of a growing number of young hikers in the UK. Nearly 9% of 16-34 year-olds are regular hill walkers or hikers, according to Sport England, up from 2.3% eight years ago.

Many young walkers' groups from Inverness to Nottinghamshire have seen their membership rise over the past two years, according to the Ramblers walking charity.

Demand has nearly doubled for a course it offers teaching map and compass skills to 18-25 year-olds.

Many who sign up want to ditch their phones and no longer rely on a blue dot to navigate, says Alistair Cooper, who leads the Out There Award programme.

"There's a cohort that missed out on outdoorsy, fun stuff during Covid. They want to get out and explore - but often don't know where to start."

Some 83% of people in the UK live in towns and cities, according to the UN, where research suggests noise, traffic, stress and information overload put huge demands on our brains, affecting our mental health.

"Nature is the environment we are adapted to, and being close to it brings benefits such as improved wellbeing, brain function and physical performance," says Dr Danny Longman, lecturer in human evolutionary physiology from Loughborough University.

"There is a theory that simply paying attention to trees and leaves allows our brains to recover," he says.

Environmental science student Deborah Odutayo, 24, described going through "an identity crisis".

"I didn't see myself as someone who works behind a desk from 9 to 5," she said.

After solo travelling, Odutayo had dreams of living abroad but didn't know how to finance them. So she decided to change her mindset.

"I just need to be outside, essentially. That's how I started like doing solo hikes and stuff. It feels very therapeutic - mostly for my mental health."

She's since hiked in Kent and the Peak District, among other locations, and camped with an outdoor group in Dorset.

Learning how to get around without using her phone or digital maps is something she is proud of, saying it feels "more intentional and grounding".

Walking gives people "an instant friend group" when life is in flux, says Miranda Chambers-Reid, who leads a Ramblers' walking group for people in their 20s and 30s in Sheffield.

"They don't want all of their friends to be work friends or old uni friends," she says.

As a mum of a seven-year-old, she made a similar decision when she joined: "I thought, I don't want all of my friends to be mum friends."

Over the last two years, the group has increased from 250 members to 350.

For some it's more about a sense of achievement says Chambers-Reid, who herself covers about 30 miles of walking a week.

"I work in an office and I can't see the sky so whenever possible I will be outside."

For Sej Chauhan, 27, her walking group is about making connections while keeping costs down.

"There's a growing interest in socialising in ways that don't involve drinking alcohol or spending lots of money," she says.

Chauhan set up Girls Who Walk in her home town of Leicester after a lonely year spent studying in Bristol.

To make that experience easier for others, the group's focus is on walking in parks, talking and female companionship. And there's always a stop for coffee.

In two years, the group has grown to more than 300 members - most are 25-35 years old.

"There's no pressure, no barriers with walking," Chauhan says. "Social media can often fill the void outside of work and home, but it doesn't provide the connection that people are craving."

articles.title: Major Thanksgiving storm brings flooding, flight delays across US
articles.text:
A massive Thanksgiving storm hammering the Midwest and north-east with heavy rain and winds, along with high tides out west, is causing widespread disruptions across the US.

More than 80 million Americans expected to be travelling this week. On Thursday 460 flights in the US were cancelled and another 2,508 flights into, out of, or within the US were delayed, tracking site FlightAware said.

The FAA has previously warned that delays would be possible "throughout the week" as a result of the rain and wind that are forecast.

Meanwhile, almost one million households were without power on Thursday night, with Pennsylvania, Maryland and Virginia the hardest hit states.

On Thursday, a powerful storm hit the eastern US, bringing damaging winds of up to 70mph, torrential rain, and major coastal flooding.

New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill declared a state of emergency as several communities along the Jersey Shore saw widespread flooding.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul also declared a state of emergency for New York City, Long Island and Westchester County.

In New York City, organisers of the annual Macy's Thanksgiving parade have postponed the event to Saturday.

Bridges closed in Maryland due to severe winds and waves battered beaches in Delaware as water seeped onto the boardwalk.

In Maryland, almost two million customers have been asked by the water utility to use water for essential use only due to "intermittent power disruptions".

On the wettest Thanksgiving on record in Washington DC, tidal waters surged and soaked runways at Reagan Washington National Airport, according to the National Water Prediction Service.

More than 980,000 households were reporting power outages by Thursday evening, with Pennsylvania, Virginia, Maryland and New Jersey hit particularly hard.

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said that utility providers were working tirelessly to restore power. Meanwhile, energy companies in Virginia and New Jersey warned it may take some time, even days, for power to return, as crews had to wait until it was safe to access damaged areas.

On Thursday afternoon, President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds for the east coast as it faces down the holiday storm.

Across the US, severe weather is also descending on the West Coast. The NWS has warned of a series of Pacific storms that are expected to bring rain, mountain snow and strong winds.

In Miami, some travel delays persisted into Thursday after a FedEx plane overshot the runway the night before, which prompted the closure of all but one runway at the airport for a brief period.

A statement FedEx provided to US media confirmed that one of its flights had "experienced an issue upon landing".

It added: "We are grateful that our crew is safe and there are no reported injuries. We are coordinating closely with investigating authorities, and any additional questions should be referred to the FAA."

An airport employee who spoke anonymously to CBS News, the BBC's US partner, raised the possibility that rainy conditions had been a factor.

"They tried as hard as they could to stop, but I don't know if it was the weather because the rain and the wind were really bad, and they just couldn't stop in time and went right off the runway and veered off into the grass," they said.

Wednesday's incident in Miami came 11 weeks after a cargo plane crashed on landing at the same airport, killing five people and injuring five others in vehicles on the ground with which it collided.

The American Automobile Association (AAA) predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for the Thanksgiving holiday over a seven-day period.

Rebecka Pieder contributed reporting.

articles.title: New Zealand election results: Ruling coalition loses parliamentary majority
articles.text:
New Zealand's ruling coalition has fallen short of a parliamentary majority by one seat, following a campaign shaped by a sluggish economy and disillusioned voters.

It now needs the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to remain in power. If they cannot reach a deal, the country may have to go back to the polls.

The incumbent National Party led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon secured 40 out of 130 seats, while its coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First took 13 and 12 respectively.

A government led by the centre-left Labour Party is not possible, official results on Friday show, as the bloc would not have enough seats even if Opportunity threw its weight behind it.

Luxon on Friday acknowledged that negotiations "may be challenging" and will take some time.

"Kiwis won't thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart or for sending them back to the polls," he told reporters.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said his party "ran an incredible campaign" but acknowledged that it doesn't have negotiating power despite winning the popular vote. "More New Zealanders voted for change at this election than for the status quo," he said.

New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions. Each person casts two votes – one for their preferred political party and another for their choice of local representative.

Labour secured 36 seats, The Greens took 17, while Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, picked up five.

Opportunity, which has been described as this election's kingmaker, secured seven seats. Opportunity's leader Qiulae Wong told reporters her party will negotiate with National, but that all options remain on the table.

"There are seven parties in parliment and everyone is responsible for making sure we do everything we can to deliver a stable government for New Zealand. It's not just up to us," she said on Friday.

Preliminary results on 7 November, election day, had projected that National combined with its coalition partners would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc.

But today's official tally shows it had lost two seats on special votes - cast by citizens who were overseas or outside of their registered electorate on election day - which typically skew left.

Some of National's key election pledges include lower taxes, cheaper energy, more renewable generation, and a greater focus on defence.

Labour, meanwhile, had campaigned to cut healthcare, public transport and fuel costs, more government support for social housing, among other things.

In earlier interviews with the BBC, many voters had expressed frustration over spiralling costs of living and high unemployment across the country, with declining faith in their political leadership.

"There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread," said 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger.

A 40-year-old man said he didn't vote as he could not bring himself to tick any of the boxes on the ballot paper.

More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to a survey by the Helen Clark Foundation, a public policy think tank.

articles.title: German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel smuggling gangs, BBC finds
articles.text:
A German boat dealer is suspected by European authorities of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers operating in the English Channel, the BBC can reveal.

Nearly a third of small-boat crossings in the first four months of this year allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen.

The managing director, Marvin Reuter, is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.

His equipment is suspected of being linked to two fatal accidents, in which four men died.

We confronted the 35-year-old at his business near Dortmund, but he would not answer our questions. He said he was reporting us to the police.

Reuter cannot be formally charged until extradited to France but could face jail time, if tried and convicted. He is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

The BBC - alongside German broadcasters WDR and NDR, newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) - and France's Le Monde newspaper - has obtained and reviewed hundreds of police, court and tax documents about the case. We have blurred images of Reuter because of German privacy rules.

Investigators, we have learned, believe they have uncovered clear, persistent links between Reuter and smuggling networks.

Evidence has been gathered through the confessions of alleged accomplices and covert jail-cell recordings of an alleged gang chief - as well as the two deadly crossing attempts.

At least 82 boats from Reuter's firm reached the English coast in just over two years to May, according to French investigations.

There are also press photos dating back five years showing the MaReBoote logo on dinghies crowded with migrants.

In 2021, Reuter told the Sun and Guardian he felt "frustrated" and "anxious" that his vessels had ended up in the hands of smugglers.

There was no suggestion, at that time, that authorities suspected him of wrongdoing as a German detective reportedly told the Sun: "This would be like if somebody buys a Mercedes and does something in another country which is wrong. The Mercedes seller can't help that."

It is not exactly clear when police suspicions were aroused.

French prosecutor Samuel Finielz would not comment on the details of the investigation but confirmed the head of a German company is currently the subject of a European Arrest Warrant.

The warrant was issued in May this year and relates to alleged offences dating back to December 2024.

While selling boats is "perfectly legal" it becomes illegal, said Finielz, "when one is fully aware that they will be used by networks involved in illegal immigration or human trafficking".

Case files we have seen say that German police had learned from UK authorities that 29% of detected crossings this year, up to the end of April, involved boats and/or engines linked to MaReBoote.

In France, five other men have already been charged as part of the investigation - an Iranian, three Iraqis and a Syrian.

In one of the two fatal incidents where Reuter's equipment is suspected to be involved, one of those who died was also Syrian.

Suliman al Husein would have just turned 20 when he died, according to a birth date listed in the files.

News reports at the time say he suffered a cardiac arrest after likely being crushed on a packed dinghy during a failed launch, west of Calais, in January 2025.

He was the first migrant to die in the English Channel that year. His body was found on the floor of the boat which, investigators allege, bore the MaReBoote logo.

The case against Reuter also stems from a chance arrest when French police pulled over a vehicle with German plates, near the northern port city of Boulogne-sur-Mer.

The BMW, which was towing a trailer, was spotted overtaking another vehicle at speed in the early hours of a morning in May this year - police records say.

Inside the car were two German nationals who - according to a subsequent search - were transporting jerry cans of fuel, a boat engine, pumps and a rolled up inflatable dinghy.

The men claimed they had been paid up to €1,000-a-time (£830) to make several, similar drops to "foreigners" on the coast, interrogation records show.

"Of course I knew that it wasn't legal," one is said to have admitted under questioning. "The money made me turn a blind eye."

Take a look at BBC Verify's UK migration tracker - the latest numbers on net migration, visas, asylum and small boats

Both men, who have since been convicted for smuggling offences, allegedly implicated Marvin Reuter as the man who had hired and paid them for this work.

Police files say both the BMW and the boat it was carrying had MaReBoote logos on them.

Marvin Reuter was arrested in Germany in May and later released, pending extradition.

On the day of his arrest, German police also seized more than 30 dinghies and 9,000 life jackets. Equipment which, we can now reveal, was allegedly linked to Reuter.

The BBC was previously granted access to see this haul, held in a police warehouse at a secret location in western Germany.

In Germany, it became explicitly illegal to aid smuggling to the UK at the end of last year after a prior BBC investigation exposed the country's role as a storage hub for gangs. Before then, some anti-smuggling laws in Germany had no longer applied to the UK because of Brexit.

The raid that saw the seizure of equipment that was allegedly linked to Reuter marked the first time the new law had been used.

Small boat crossings have dropped significantly in 2026, with British authorities citing law enforcement as a "key factor". However, illegal migration into Europe has also been falling.

The UK National Crime Agency's (NCA) deputy director for organized immigration crime, Dan Cannatella-Barcroft, praised Germany's "commitment" to tackling people-smuggling but acknowledged the country would remain "an important piece of the puzzle".

While a gap in the law has been closed, Germany's proximity to France, wider transport links and the fact that some of the Kurdish-dominated gangs are based there, means it is expected to stay as a transit point in the illegal small-boats trade.

The "vast majority" of small boats equipment in the past few years has come through Germany, Cannatella-Barcroft told the BBC - much of it made in China and having been routed through Turkey.
